author: Fowler
title: Trimming Knowledge for Gains: Distilling Language Models Layer by Layer with Task Awareness
abstract: Compressing bulky teacher models down to compact student models can be accomplished effectively through layer-wise distillation, in which the student acquires knowledge by reproducing the teacher's hidden representations at each intermediate layer. Yet this procedure poses obstacles. Because a student has lower model capacity relative to its teacher, under-fitting frequently occurs. On top of that, the teacher's hidden representations carry redundant information that is not strictly required by the student when learning the target task. We introduce a new method to overcome these issues. The proposed approach builds task-aware filters that bring the student's and teacher's hidden representations into alignment at every layer, with the filters isolating, from the hidden representations, only the knowledge relevant to the target task. Through this mechanism, the gap in knowledge separating the two models shrinks, and the student is better able to fit the target task. Two settings serve for evaluation: continual pre-training as well as fine-tuning. In each of these settings, the proposed method yields substantial and reliable gains beyond prior distillation methods. Code is released at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

author: Johnson
title: Reducing Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models Through Counterfactual Role Swapping
abstract: While language models are highly capable of producing fluent text, deployment under limited computational resources has become feasible thanks to compression strategies like knowledge distillation. Such models, however, are prone to various forms of bias—for instance, incorrectly linking gender-neutral occupations to male or female genders. As a consequence, applying knowledge distillation absent any fairness objectives risks carrying over, or even amplifying, the biases of the teacher model into the distilled one. Motivated by this, we introduce a new technique that trains for fairness during knowledge distillation so as to lessen gender imbalance in generated text. Building on standard knowledge distillation, we suggest two changes grounded in counterfactual role reversal: altering the teacher probabilities and enriching the training set. Using open-ended text produced by the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT-2 models, we measure gender polarity across occupations and show that gender imbalance drops considerably while utility declines only slightly. Lastly, we find that language models achieving lower gender polarity in text generation do not yield gains in either embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

author: Hill
title: A Hierarchical Deep Framework for Lifelong Learning within Minecraft
abstract: Here we introduce a lifelong learning system capable of transferring and reusing knowledge across tasks, all while effectively preserving what it has previously learned. We accomplish this transfer through the acquisition of reusable skills aimed at solving tasks in Minecraft, a widely played video game that constitutes a high-dimensional and as-yet unsolved lifelong learning challenge. We term these reusable skills Deep Skill Networks, and they are embedded into the proposed hierarchical deep reinforcement learning architecture by means of two mechanisms: first, a deep skill array, and second, skill distillation, which is our own adaptation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) applied to skill learning. By gathering knowledge and packing several reusable skills into one distilled network, skill distillation lets the architecture retain knowledge efficiently and thus scale in the lifelong learning setting. Across sub-domains of Minecraft, the proposed architecture achieves better performance together with reduced learning sample complexity relative to the standard Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015).

author: Walker
title: Teaching-Aware BERT: A Meta Learning Perspective on Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Unlike conventional knowledge distillation (KD) approaches, which keep the teacher model frozen throughout training, the proposed method offers a straightforward yet effective alternative that couples KD with meta learning. Within a meta learning framework, we demonstrate that signals derived from how well the distilled student network performs allow the teacher network to acquire the skill of transferring knowledge more effectively to the student network—in other words, learning to teach. We additionally propose a pilot update procedure that strengthens the correspondence between the inner-learner and the meta-learner, targeting meta learning algorithms designed to enhance the inner-learner. Across a range of benchmarks, our experiments indicate that the method delivers notable gains over traditional KD algorithms while showing reduced sensitivity to variations in student capacity and hyperparameters, thereby making KD easier to apply across diverse tasks and models.

author: Doyle
title: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender Systems Using Latent Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Knowledge distillation—a model compression technique in which knowledge is passed from a bulky model (teacher) to a lightweight model (student)—has recently found use in recommender systems as a way to keep performance intact while cutting inference latency. Existing top-performing approaches concentrate solely on training the student model to faithfully reproduce the teacher model's predictions. Because the prediction outputs only partially expose what the teacher knows, such approaches are limited. We introduce in this work a new knowledge distillation framework for recommender systems, referred to here as the proposed method, through which the student model draws not only on the teacher's predictions but also on the latent knowledge held within the teacher model. Specifically, the framework combines two techniques: 1) a component that transfers latent knowledge straight from the teacher model, employing "experts" together with a new strategy for selecting experts so that the teacher's extensive knowledge is effectively distilled into the capacity-limited student; and 2) a component that conveys the knowledge exposed by the teacher's prediction while accounting for relaxed ranking orders across items. Through comprehensive experiments we demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses the leading competitors and, with reduced inference time, attains performance on par with or exceeding that of the teacher model.

author: Rhodes
title: Distilling Knowledge for Lifelong Language Learning
abstract: Handling a sequence of distinct tasks through lifelong language learning (LLL), while matching the performance of multi-task alternatives without any drop, remains a difficult problem. We introduce the proposed method, a straightforward yet effective approach that plugs easily into current LLL architectures to reduce such performance loss. In particular, whenever the LLL model encounters a new task during training, a teacher model is first tasked with mastering it, and its knowledge is then transferred to the LLL model through knowledge distillation. This allows the LLL model to adapt to the incoming task without discarding what it has already learned. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method reliably surpasses prior state-of-the-art models, and that the drop relative to multi-task models on LLL tasks is substantially reduced across both text classification and sequence generation settings.

author: Mcclain
title: Distilling Knowledge from a Model's Internal Representations
abstract: Usually, knowledge distillation proceeds by having a compact model (the student) learn to reproduce the behavior of a bulky, unwieldy model (the teacher). Here the goal is to transfer the teacher's knowledge by treating its output probabilities as soft-labels against which the student is optimized. Yet when the teacher is quite large, nothing ensures that its internal knowledge actually reaches the student: a student that fits the soft-labels well may still form internal representations that differ substantially. Such a discrepancy on the inside can weaken the generalization capabilities that the transfer from teacher to student was meant to preserve. We propose in this work to distill the internal representations of a large model like BERT into a streamlined counterpart. Two schemes for distilling these representations are formulated, together with several algorithms for carrying out the distillation. Across datasets drawn from the GLUE benchmark, our experiments repeatedly demonstrate that incorporating knowledge distillation from internal representations outperforms relying on soft-label distillation alone.

author: Miller
title: Enhancing Spoken Question Answering Accuracy Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: To succeed at spoken question answering (SQA), a machine must achieve a thorough comprehension of intricate spoken documents, which makes it a demanding problem. Within QA systems, automatic speech recognition (ASR) is a key component. Recent studies, however, reveal that the transcripts produced by ASR systems are extremely noisy, and this severely constrains how well machine comprehension performs on SQA. We propose a new distillation framework to tackle this problem. In particular, our training strategy carries out knowledge distillation (KD) using both spoken documents and their written counterparts. By narrowing the discrepancy between manual and automatic transcriptions, our work advances the idea of distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal, thereby yielding improved student accuracy. On the Spoken-SQuAD dataset, our experiments show that the proposed approach surpasses several state-of-the-art language models.

author: Henderson
title: Compressing Model Ensembles into a Single Network through Adversarial Learning
abstract: Ensembles built from several base-level networks frequently yield the strongest deep neural models. Their practical adoption is limited, however, because holding all of these networks in memory and running them during testing becomes infeasible when test collections are sizable, as with ImageNet. Here we describe an approach that condenses a bulky, elaborate trained ensemble down to one network, distilling the knowledge held across an assortment of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) and transferring it into a single DNN. To pull diverse knowledge out of the various trained (teacher) models, we adopt an adversarial-based learning strategy: a block-wise training loss steers and tunes a predefined student network toward recovering what the teacher models know, while at the same time encouraging the discriminator network to tell teacher features apart from student features. This adversarial scheme for conveying distilled knowledge, which we introduce here, brings three notable benefits: (1) with the aid of discriminators, the student network that absorbs the distilled knowledge ends up better optimized than the original model; (2) a single forward pass delivers fast inference, yet the accuracy surpasses that of conventional ensembles assembled from multiple original models; (3) the student network is able to acquire distilled knowledge regardless of the teacher model's structure. Thorough experiments across CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet confirm that the proposed method is effective. Using ResNet-50 on ImageNet, the proposed method attains top-1/5 val error of 21.79%/5.99%, beating the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models can be found at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

author: Robinson
title: Training Teacher Networks Amenable to Students for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: To ease how dark knowledge moves from a teacher into a student, this work introduces a new knowledge distillation scheme. Whereas the bulk of prior work assumes a pretrained teacher and concentrates on training the student well, our objective instead is to produce teacher models that suit students and are therefore better fits for transferring knowledge. Put differently, while a teacher model is being optimized, the proposed method simultaneously trains student branches so that student-friendly representations emerge. Because the central aim is the training of teacher models, and the knowledge distillation step that follows remains simple, this technique can be incorporated by most existing knowledge distillation methods to boost the accuracy and convergence speed of a range of student models. Across several well-established knowledge distillation techniques and many teacher–student pairings, the proposed algorithm attains excellent accuracy, holding even when the architectures differ and no information about the student models is available while the teacher networks are trained.

author: Wagner
title: Distilling Knowledge from a Model's Own Predictions for Natural Language Processing
abstract: Following the rise of deep learning as a central approach within natural language processing (NLP), numerous deep learning models have achieved impressive results across a wide range of NLP tasks, occasionally surpassing human-level performance. The efficiency with which these models represent knowledge accounts for this strong performance. Although a variety of techniques have been introduced to obtain more efficient representations, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks indicates that the soft target probability carries additional information usable for training other neural networks. Here we introduce a novel knowledge distillation approach, self-knowledge distillation, that relies on the soft target probabilities generated by the training model itself, distilling multimode information out of the word embedding space located directly beneath the softmax layer. Because of time complexity concerns, the proposed method uses an approximation of the soft target probabilities. For our experiments, we tested this technique on two core and distinct NLP tasks, namely language modeling and neural machine translation. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method yields gains in performance on both tasks.

author: Johnson
title: Wide Neural Networks and Knowledge Distillation: Bounding Risk, Efficiency of Data, and the Imperfect Teacher
abstract: By using the soft output of a teacher network to guide the training of a student network, knowledge distillation has proven effective for both transferring knowledge and compressing models. Yet a solid theoretical account of why it works remains missing. Meanwhile, the neural tangent kernel now lets us treat a wide neural network as a linear model built on the network's random features. Drawing on this, we carry out a theoretical study of knowledge distillation in the wide neural network regime. We begin by deriving a transfer risk bound for the linearized version of the network. We next introduce a measure of how hard a task is to train on, which we term data inefficiency. Using this measure, we demonstrate that when the teacher is perfect, weighting the teacher's soft labels heavily can help. Turning to the imperfect teacher, we observe that hard labels are able to fix mistaken predictions made by the teacher, offering an account of why hard and soft labels are commonly combined in practice.

author: Gonzalez
title: Emphasizing Each Stage: Knowledge Distillation through Collaborative Teaching
abstract: Deploying deep neural networks onto devices with limited resources is hindered by their demanding memory and computation requirements. To address this, knowledge distillation seeks to build a lightweight student network by conveying knowledge from a bigger pre-trained teacher. Yet the majority of current knowledge distillation approaches overlook the useful information contained in the training process alongside its outcomes. Here we introduce a new collaborative teaching strategy for knowledge distillation that relies on two distinct teachers. In particular, a teacher learned from the ground up (the scratch teacher) supports the student progressively through its intermediate outputs, driving the student along an optimal trajectory toward the final logits with high accuracy. Meanwhile, a second pre-trained teacher (the expert teacher) directs the student's attention to a crucial region that is more beneficial for the task. By merging the knowledge supplied by these two distinct teachers, the student network's performance in knowledge distillation can be markedly enhanced. Experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets confirm that the proposed knowledge distillation method is effective and reaches state-of-the-art performance.

author: Santos
title: Channel-Wise Attention as a Mechanism for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The goal of knowledge distillation is to move the knowledge that a teacher network has acquired from data into a student network, giving the student fewer parameters and a lighter computational cost while keeping its accuracy near that of the teacher. Here we introduce a novel distillation approach composed of two transfer strategies together with a strategy for decaying the loss. Grounded in channel-wise attention, the first transfer strategy—which we refer to as the proposed channel-based scheme—passes channel information from the teacher to the student. The second strategy is a guided variant of distillation: whereas standard Knowledge Distillation (KD) has the student imitate the teacher's prediction distribution over every sample, this guided version restricts the student to imitating only the teacher's correct output. The final component gradually lowers the weight assigned to the distillation loss as training proceeds, so that control over the optimization is handed progressively from the teacher to the student. We test the method on ImageNet and CIFAR100. Using ResNet18 on ImageNet, we reach a top-1 error of 27.68%, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100 we obtain the striking outcome that the student surpasses the teacher. Code can be found at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

author: Gardner
title: Distillation That Preserves Robustness Against Adversarial Attacks
abstract: Compact, high-performance classification networks can be built through knowledge distillation, yet such compact models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. Here we examine the way adversarial robustness is conveyed from teacher to student throughout knowledge distillation. Our first observation is that the student can acquire a considerable degree of robustness even if distillation uses clean images alone. We then propose a method for transferring robustness to student networks. Beyond delivering compact models with strong test accuracy, as ordinary distillation does, the proposed approach additionally hands down the greater robustness of the large networks to the student. Experimentally, students trained with our method clearly beat adversarially trained networks sharing the same architecture on robust accuracy, exceeding state-of-the-art techniques across common robustness benchmarks. Lastly, we tailor recent fast adversarial training schemes to our method so that robust distillation runs faster.

author: Robinson
title: A Theoretical Investigation of Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation, and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
abstract: This work provides a rigorous analysis of the mechanism by which an ensemble of deep learning models raises test accuracy, along with how knowledge distillation transfers this improved performance into a single model. Our focus is the demanding setting in which the ensemble amounts to nothing more than averaging the outputs of several neural networks that share the SAME architecture, were trained by the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and are distinguished only through the random seeds governing their initialization. We demonstrate that, in Deep Learning, ensemble and knowledge distillation behave in a manner sharply distinct from what traditional learning theory (for instance boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels) predicts. Toward a correct account of these phenomena, we construct a theory establishing that, under a data property we call ``multi-view'', an ensemble of independently trained neural networks provably raises test accuracy, and that this improved test accuracy can provably be distilled into a single model when that model is trained to reproduce the ensemble's output rather than the ground-truth label. These findings clarify how ensemble operates in deep learning in a fashion entirely unlike classical results, and reveal how the ``dark knowledge'' embedded within the ensemble's outputs serves distillation. Finally, we prove that self-distillation may itself be understood as an implicit fusion of ensemble and knowledge distillation that enhances test accuracy.

author: Lawrence
title: Transferring Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network via Distillation
abstract: We introduce a new approach for producing efficient Visual Odometry (VO) by distilling knowledge out of a deep pose regressor network. Conventional distillation depends on "dark knowledge" to make the transfer of knowledge work. Because such knowledge does not exist for pose regression, and because the teacher does not always predict accurately, our idea is to stress knowledge transfer selectively, only in cases where the teacher is trustworthy. To do so, we treat the teacher loss as a confidence score, thereby assigning different relative weight to what the teacher predicts. This confidence score is fed into the primary training objective through the proposed attentive imitation loss, as well as into the learning of the teacher's intermediate representation via the proposed attentive hint training scheme. As far as we know, this constitutes the first successful distillation of knowledge out of a deep pose regression network. Experiments conducted on the KITTI and Malaga dataset demonstrate that the student prediction stays near the teacher while achieving as much as 92.95% fewer parameters and computation that runs 2.12x faster.

author: Pacheco
title: Supporting the Decision Boundary via Adversarial Samples for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Although numerous studies have recently introduced schemes for passing the knowledge held by a trained network to aid the training of another, the search for an effective knowledge distillation technique remains unsolved. Here we offer a fresh viewpoint grounded in the decision boundary, a component that ranks among the most crucial in any classifier. Because how well a classifier generalizes depends heavily on how suitable its decision boundary is, a strong classifier possesses a strong decision boundary. Consequently, conveying information tied closely to the decision boundary could serve as a worthwhile approach to knowledge distillation. We accomplish this by employing an adversarial attack to locate samples that support a decision boundary. Building on this notion, the algorithm we propose trains a student classifier from the adversarial samples that support the decision boundary, thereby conveying more precise information about it. Our experiments demonstrate that the method does enhance knowledge distillation and reaches state-of-the-art performance.

author: Smith
title: Interpreting Knowledge Distillation Through Measurement of the Encoded Knowledge
abstract: By measuring and examining the task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts represented within the intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN), this paper offers an approach for understanding why knowledge distillation works. In particular, we put forward the following three hypotheses. 1. Compared to training directly on raw data, knowledge distillation causes the DNN to acquire a greater number of visual concepts. 2. Under knowledge distillation, the DNN tends to pick up multiple visual concepts at once, while training from raw data leads the DNN to acquire visual concepts one after another. 3. The optimization directions produced by knowledge distillation are more stable than those obtained from raw data. To assess the feature representations of the DNN in line with these ideas, we construct three categories of mathematical metrics. We then applied diagnostics to a range of DNNs in our experiments, which confirmed the hypotheses stated above.

author: Shaffer
title: Choosing Which Samples Matter: Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: On numerous translation benchmarks, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models reach state-of-the-art performance. Within this vibrant NMT research area, knowledge distillation sees broad use, improving a model by carrying the teacher model's knowledge across each training sample. That said, the varying roles and relationships of these samples—the conduits through which teacher knowledge passes—have seldom been examined in earlier studies. Here, we introduce a fresh protocol that, through comparison of different partitions of the samples, is able to dissect how individual samples exert distinct effects. Running comprehensive experiments under this protocol, we observe that having more teacher knowledge does not guarantee better outcomes; on certain samples, such knowledge can actually degrade the overall effectiveness of knowledge distillation. To resolve this, we put forward two straightforward but potent selection strategies operating at the batch level and the global level, respectively, which identify the appropriate samples for distillation. Testing on two large-scale machine translation tasks, namely WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English, our methods deliver gains of as much as +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points over the Transformer baseline.

author: Wolfe
title: Toward Robust, Memory-Light Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via a Generative Pseudo Replay Scheme
abstract: When the original training data is unavailable, Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) still enables transferring knowledge from a trained neural network (teacher) into a smaller student network. Prior approaches typically rely on a validation set to track how well the student performs on real data, subsequently reporting the best accuracy observed across the run. Yet a validation set might likewise be missing during distillation, which makes it impractical to capture the particular student snapshot corresponding to peak accuracy. For this reason, a usable data-free KD scheme ought to be robust, and preferably yield student accuracy that rises monotonically as distillation proceeds. Achieving this is difficult, since the distribution shift of the synthetic data causes the student to undergo knowledge degradation. One obvious remedy—periodically saving and rehearsing the generated samples—inflates the memory footprint while raising privacy concerns. Instead, we model the distribution of synthetic samples seen earlier using a generative network. Concretely, we build a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) whose training objective is tailored so that it optimally captures representations of the synthetic data. Rehearsing the student proceeds through the generative pseudo replay technique using samples the VAE generates, so that knowledge degradation is averted while no samples need to be stored. On image classification benchmarks, our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method maximizes the expected accuracy of the distilled model and removes the substantial memory overhead that sample-storing methods incur.

author: Peterson
title: Investigating the Role of Knowledge Distillation for Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
abstract: By generating output tokens simultaneously rather than one after another, non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems deliver considerable speedups relative to autoregressive counterparts. To reach competitive performance, most current NAT models depend on knowledge distillation, in which training data is generated by a pretrained autoregressive model. Although this practice consistently yields sizable accuracy improvements for NAT models in practice, what drives the effect has remained unclear so far. We begin by constructing controlled experiments aimed at explaining why knowledge distillation matters so much for training NAT. Our analysis shows that knowledge distillation lowers how complex the data sets are, thereby making it easier for NAT to capture the output variations. We additionally find a strong link between an NAT model's capacity and the level of distilled-data complexity that yields the best translation quality. Building on these observations, we introduce several methods for adjusting data set complexity so as to boost NAT model performance. On the WMT14 En-De benchmark we obtain state-of-the-art results among NAT-based models and narrow the distance to the autoregressive baseline.

author: Moore
title: Distillation of Knowledge through Attention-Guided Feature Matching
abstract: To guide a target student network, knowledge distillation draws general knowledge out of a teacher network that has been pre-trained. In the majority of prior work, intermediate features of student and teacher are bound by hand, with knowledge passed along links that are fixed in advance. Such hand-crafted choices, however, frequently yield links that are ineffective and thereby cap the gains achievable through distillation. Although this issue has previously been tackled, pinpointing effective links in realistic settings remains difficult. Here we present a feature distillation method that is both efficient and effective, drawing on every feature level of the teacher while avoiding any manual link selection. Concretely, the proposed method relies on an attention-based meta-network that learns the relative similarities among features, then uses those learned similarities to modulate distillation intensities across all candidate pairs. Consequently, compared with the earlier approach, our method pinpoints capable links with greater efficiency and yields stronger results on both transfer learning and model compression tasks. We further include ablative studies and qualitative analyses that explain the source of the improved distillation. Implementation code can be found at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Dynamic Teacher Weighting via Reinforcement for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deploying pre-trained deep models in production settings for natural language processing (NLP) tasks is hindered by their sluggish inference and their substantial demands on GPU memory. Knowledge distillation, widely adopted to compress models, moves knowledge out of one or several large (teacher) models and into a compact (student) model. Current leading approaches, when several teacher models participate, keep each teacher model's weight constant throughout the entire distillation process, and the majority of them go further by weighting every teacher model identically. Our study finds that, because training examples vary in difficulty and the student model has limited capability, drawing on teacher models in an uneven manner can yield distilled student models that perform better. To this end, we methodically construct a reinforced approach that adaptively sets teacher model weights per training instance while optimizing student model performance. Comprehensive experiments across multiple NLP tasks provide clear evidence for the practicality and effectiveness of the proposed method.

author: Rogers
title: Reliability-Guided Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Teachers
abstract: Originally, knowledge distillation was proposed as a way to provide the student model with extra supervisory signals drawn from one teacher model during training. Seeking better student performance, several newer approaches have turned to harvesting varied knowledge across a collection of teachers. The trouble is that current work typically fuses these varied sources either by taking the mean of the different teacher predictions or by applying assorted label-free combination schemes, and such fusion can steer the student astray whenever some teacher predictions are of poor quality. We address this issue with the proposed method, which leverages ground-truth labels to adaptively estimate a per-sample reliability score for every teacher prediction, granting greater weight to those teacher predictions that lie near the one-hot labels. The proposed method additionally draws on intermediate layers so as to stabilize the transfer of knowledge. Through extensive experiments, we find that our approach consistently surpasses every state-of-the-art baseline it is compared against, holding across a range of teacher-student architectures.

author: Davis
title: Adversarial Online Knowledge Distillation at the Feature-map Level
abstract: Although feature maps encode abundant details regarding spatial correlation and image intensity, existing online knowledge distillation approaches rely solely on the class probabilities. To address this, we introduce in this work an online knowledge distillation technique built on the adversarial training framework, which conveys both the knowledge held in the class probabilities and that held in the feature map. Several networks are trained at once, with discriminators tasked to tell apart the feature map distributions belonging to distinct networks. A dedicated discriminator is assigned to every network; it labels the feature map coming from its associated network as fake while treating the one from the other network as real. Because a network is optimized to deceive its paired discriminator, it acquires the feature map distribution of the counterpart network. Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses standard direct alignment schemes like L1 and fits online distillation more appropriately. Additionally, we put forward a new cyclic learning strategy that enables the joint training of more than two networks. Applying the method to a range of network architectures on the classification task, we observe a marked gain in performance, most notably when a small network is trained alongside a large one.

author: Abbott
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation for Shrinking Deep Graph Neural Networks
abstract: When it comes to representing data organized as graphs, deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated strong expressive power. The problem is that their heavily stacked layers hinder deployment and quick evaluation on embedded or mobile devices. Knowledge distillation built around a teacher-student architecture has proven useful for compressing such over-stacked GNNs; here, a distance function defined in advance quantifies how far apart the teacher and student networks are. Yet applying one fixed distance across graphs whose structures differ can be inappropriate, and settling on the best distance formulation remains challenging. We address these issues with a new adversarial knowledge distillation framework for graph models, in which a generator and a discriminator are trained adversarially so that the discrepancy is detected and reduced in an adaptive manner. Because the effectiveness of deep GNNs relies on faithfully captured inter-node and inter-class correlations, our approach employs a trainable discriminator to scrutinize the transferred knowledge from both node-level and class-level perspectives. This discriminator tells apart the teacher's knowledge from that acquired by the student, whereas the student GNN plays the role of a generator seeking to deceive the discriminator. As far as we know, the proposed method is the first to bring adversarial training into knowledge distillation within graph domains. Across benchmarks for classification at the node level and the graph level, our experiments show that the proposed method lifts student performance substantially. These findings indicate that knowledge can be accurately conveyed from an intricate teacher GNN to a lightweight student GNN.

author: Munoz
title: Distilling Knowledge Without Data in Deep Networks
abstract: The goal of knowledge distillation is to build a compact model (Student) that inherits nearly all of the capabilities of a larger, high-capacity source (Teacher). Prior work relies on the training data itself, or on meta-data derived from it, to guide the Student. Gaining access to the corpus used to fit the Teacher, however, is not always possible when that corpus is enormous or raises safety and privacy issues (for instance, medical or bio-metric records). Motivated by this, we introduce a new data-free approach for transferring knowledge from the Teacher to the Student. Even in the absence of meta-data, we generate what we call Data Impressions from the intricate Teacher model, then treat these as stand-ins for genuine training samples, passing on the Teacher's learning to the Student through knowledge distillation. We refer to the proposed method accordingly, and across several benchmark datasets we show that it attains generalization performance on par with distillation carried out using the real training data.

author: Roman
title: Distillation of Features for Equitable Visual Recognition
abstract: In computer vision, and particularly within systems that make decisions concerning people, fairness has emerged as a matter of growing importance. Yet the goal of algorithmic fairness—ensuring that a model does not treat protected groups differently in its outputs—remains an open challenge. Here we propose a principled framework, based on MMD, that curbs algorithmic biases through feature distillation applied to visual recognition tasks. Although distillation has long served as a means of raising prediction accuracy in general, to our knowledge no prior study has explicitly leveraged distillation to enhance fairness as well. We additionally provide theoretical grounding that clarifies how knowledge distillation relates to fairness for the proposed method. Across a broad set of experiments spanning both synthetic and real-world face datasets, we demonstrate that our approach substantially lessens bias toward particular minorities while incurring no drop in accuracy.

author: Blair
title: An Examination of Policy Distillation Approaches
abstract: Within Deep Reinforcement Learning, moving knowledge from a source policy into a target one constitutes a valuable technique. Known as distillation, this procedure has yielded notable gains—for instance, it improves how agents are optimised, so that on more difficult domains they reach greater performance more rapidly [26, 32, 5, 8]. Although distillation is conceptually simple and broadly adopted, practitioners rely on numerous distinct formulations, and even minor differences among these can dramatically alter both performance and the underlying objective being optimised. Here we systematically survey the full space of policy distillation, weighing the rationale and merits of every variant via both theoretical and empirical study. According to our findings, three distillation techniques stand out, with the best choice hinging on the particulars of the task. In particular, a distillation regularised by expected entropy, which we introduce, supports faster learning across many scenarios while continuing to guarantee convergence.

author: Herrera
title: Fine-grained Feature Imitation for the Distillation of Object Detectors
abstract: Deploying leading CNN based recognition models on low-end devices is frequently infeasible due to their heavy computation. Knowledge distillation offers an encouraging high level route around this obstacle: a compact student model learns to reproduce the output of an unwieldy teacher model, thereby achieving better generalization. Existing work along these lines, however, is largely restricted to the straightforward classification setting and overlooks harder problems such as object detection. When the plain form of knowledge distillation is transferred to a detection model, we find only marginal improvement. To overcome the difficulty of distilling knowledge for detection, we introduce a fine-grained feature imitation approach that draws on how feature response varies across locations. The reasoning behind this is that detectors are chiefly concerned with local regions surrounding objects; consequently, variation in feature response at anchor locations close to objects exposes crucial cues about the teacher model's generalization tendencies. We devise a new procedure to identify such locations and have the student model imitate the teacher at them so as to raise performance. The concept is first confirmed on a purpose-built lightweight toy detector that embodies the most basic idea underlying today's leading anchor based detection models, tested on the demanding KITTI dataset, where the proposed method yields as much as a 15% gain in mAP for the student model over its non-imitated version. Following this, we carry out broad evaluations using the Faster R-CNN model across a range of settings on the standard Pascal VOC and COCO object detection benchmarks, and imitation recovers up to 74% of the student model's performance gap relative to the teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

author: Dudley
title: Distilling Answers Through Attention Guidance for Machine Reading Comprehension
abstract: Reading comprehension systems have made considerable progress recently, yet their strong results typically depend on combining many models into an ensemble. A further weakness of current techniques is their susceptibility to adversarial attacks. To address these issues, we turn to knowledge distillation, a technique for transferring knowledge from an ensemble model into a single model. As a starting point, we show that applying vanilla knowledge distillation to answer span prediction benefits reading comprehension systems. Building on this, we introduce two novel approaches that both discourage predictions on confusing answers and steer training using alignment information distilled from the ensemble. In our experiments, the best student model runs 12x faster at inference and loses only 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set relative to the ensemble teacher. On adversarial SQuAD datasets and the NarrativeQA benchmark, it even surpasses the teacher.

author: Gray
title: Shrinking BERT via Gradual Module Substitution
abstract: This work introduces a new technique for model compression that reduces the size of BERT through gradual module substitution. The method begins by partitioning the original BERT into a set of modules, for each of which a compact substitute is constructed. During training, the original modules are swapped out at random for these substitutes, so that the compact modules learn to reproduce the behavior of their originals. As training proceeds, the likelihood of substitution is raised progressively. Through this mechanism, the technique achieves a deeper level of interaction between the compact and original models. Unlike earlier knowledge distillation methods aimed at compressing BERT, the proposed approach adds no extra loss function. On the GLUE benchmark, it surpasses existing knowledge distillation methods, offering a fresh perspective on model compression.

author: Arnold
title: Is Knowledge Distillation Actually Effective?
abstract: To train a compact student network that reproduces the behavior of a bigger teacher model—for instance an ensemble of networks—practitioners frequently rely on knowledge distillation. Our findings indicate that, although generalization of the student can benefit from knowledge distillation, the mechanism at play differs from the prevailing intuition: the predictive distributions of the student and the teacher tend to diverge by a surprisingly wide margin, and this holds even when the student possesses sufficient capacity to reproduce the teacher exactly. We trace a primary cause of this failure to match the teacher back to optimization challenges. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the choice of dataset employed during distillation affects the fidelity with which the student tracks the teacher—yet, counterintuitively, achieving a tighter match with the teacher does not necessarily improve the student's generalization.

author: Calderon
title: Toward Generalizable Vehicle Routing Solvers Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: When deep models are applied to vehicle routing problems, recent neural approaches typically rely on a single instance distribution (namely, uniform) for both training and evaluation. This raises generalization difficulties across distributions, which we address by introducing knowledge distillation into this domain through a proposed scheme that adaptively distills from multiple distributions to build deep models with broader applicability. In our design, a compact yet generalist student model is produced by drawing diverse knowledge from several teachers, each trained on a representative distribution. In addition, an adaptive mechanism directs the student toward the distributions it finds challenging, enabling it to more effectively absorb knowledge that is hard to master. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that, relative to baseline neural methods, the proposed method attains competitive performance on previously unseen instances that are either in-distribution or out-of-distribution, whether these instances are synthesized at random or drawn from benchmark datasets (namely, TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Importantly, the method is generic and requires fewer computational resources during inference.

author: Montgomery
title: Detecting 3D Objects with Dynamic Graph Networks on Point Clouds
abstract: Substantial dataset-specific expertise is typically demanded by the elaborate training and inference workflows that characterize 3D object detection. Drawing on recent 2D detectors that dispense with non-maximum suppression, we introduce an architecture for detecting 3D objects within point clouds. By treating 3D object detection as message passing across a dynamic graph, our approach extends the DGCNN framework so that it yields a collection of objects. This design eliminates any reliance on post-processing steps such as non-maximum suppression or the aggregation of object confidence scores. Because point clouds are sparse, we additionally introduce a set-to-set distillation scheme tailored for 3D detection. Operating in a permutation-invariant manner, this scheme matches the teacher model's outputs to those of the student model, which greatly streamlines knowledge distillation for 3D detection. On autonomous driving benchmarks, the proposed method reaches state-of-the-art results. We further supply extensive analysis covering both the detection model and the distillation framework.

author: Hensley
title: Boosting the Accuracy of Low-Precision Networks Through Knowledge Distillation Methods
abstract: On computer vision tasks such as object detection and image classification, deep learning networks reach the best accuracies reported to date. Yet the systems that deliver this performance generally rely on large models carrying many parameters. After training, deploying these leading models on inference systems with limited resources becomes difficult, since such models—frequently deep, or wide, or both—demand substantial compute and memory. To reduce the compute cost as well as the memory footprint of the deployed models, two widely used techniques are low-precision numerics and model compression via knowledge distillation. Here we investigate how these two techniques work together, demonstrating that knowledge distillation techniques can markedly raise the performance of low-precision networks. For variants of the ResNet architecture evaluated on the ImageNet dataset, the proposed method attains state-of-the-art accuracies at both ternary precision and 4-bit precision. We describe three schemes that allow knowledge distillation techniques to be introduced at different stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

author: Ray
title: Conveying Inductive Biases via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: In settings constrained by limited data or computing resources, or when the training distribution fails to fully match test-time conditions, possessing suitable inductive biases can prove decisive across numerous tasks. Yet the tasks of specifying, engineering, and effectively tailoring such inductive biases are far from trivial. Here we investigate how knowledge distillation can carry the influence of inductive biases from one model over to a second model. Within tasks and scenarios where the correct inductive biases matter greatly, we examine pairs of model families that differ in their inductive biases, namely LSTMs against Transformers and CNNs against MLPs. We analyze how inductive biases shape the solutions to which models converge, and we probe the degree to which knowledge distillation conveys their influence, considering not merely performance but also various properties of the converged solutions.

author: Bush
title: Boosting Multi-Label Image Classification through Knowledge Distillation from a Weakly-Supervised Detector
abstract: Assigning multiple labels to an image is a core yet difficult problem on the path to broad visual understanding. Prior work has shown that region-level cues—such as features drawn from RoIs—are helpful for multi-label classification. However, learning object-level visual features effectively through these approaches typically demands costly object-level annotations, namely object labels together with bounding boxes. Here we introduce an efficient new deep framework that enhances multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from a weakly-supervised detection task that dispenses with bounding box annotations. Concretely, relying only on image-level annotations, we (1) train a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and (2) build an end-to-end framework for multi-label image classification enriched with a knowledge distillation module, through which the WSD model steers the classification model using both the class-level predictions over the entire image and the object-level visual features associated with object RoIs. Within this scheme the WSD model serves as the teacher and the classification model as the student. Once this cross-task knowledge distillation is complete, the classification model attains markedly better performance while remaining efficient, because the WSD model can be discarded without harm at test time. Comprehensive experiments on two large-scale datasets, MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE, demonstrate that our framework surpasses the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both performance and efficiency.

author: Williams
title: Distilling Relational Knowledge for Link Prediction Without Links
abstract: On the link prediction task, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve remarkable results. Their deployment in practice is nevertheless hindered by substantial latency, which stems from the costly dependency on neighborhood data. MLPs, by contrast, are recognized for their efficiency but trail GNNs considerably because they possess no relational knowledge. Seeking to unite what GNNs and MLPs each do well, we first investigate applying knowledge distillation (KD) to link prediction in its direct forms, namely matching based on predicted logits and matching based on node representations. Since these straightforward KD counterparts turn out to be ineffective for link prediction, we introduce a relational KD framework, the proposed method, which transfers knowledge to MLPs for link prediction. Rather than aligning node representations or link logits in isolation as basic KD does, the proposed method conveys to the student MLP relational knowledge organized around each individual (anchor) node. Concretely, we put forward matching by rank and matching by distribution, two strategies that work in a complementary fashion. Through comprehensive experiments, we show the proposed method lifts MLP link prediction performance by wide margins, surpassing even the teacher GNNs on 7 of 8 benchmarks. Relative to GNNs, it further delivers a 70.68x acceleration of link prediction inference on the large-scale OGB dataset.

author: Perez
title: Adapting Across Domains Using One or Several Black-box Predictors
abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) seeks to carry knowledge from earlier, related labeled datasets (sources) over to a fresh unlabeled dataset (target), thereby reducing annotation effort. Although notable advances have been made, existing techniques typically require entry to the raw source data and build data-dependent alignment schemes that identify target samples through transductive learning, an approach that could trigger privacy worries among source individuals. To sidestep this, a number of recent works make use of a fully trained white-box model originating from the source domain; even so, the raw data may still be exposed via generative adversarial learning. Here we investigate an appealing and realistic UDA scenario in which, throughout adaptation on the target domain, one has access solely to black-box source models—that is, nothing beyond the network predictions. We address this by introducing a two-stage knowledge adaptation framework. Accounting for how the target data is structured, the proposed method begins by distilling knowledge out of the source predictor into a tailored target model, and subsequently fine-tunes that distilled model so it better matches the target domain. Moreover, the framework does not demand that neural networks be the same across domains, which even permits successful adaptation on a low-resource device. Experiments spanning three UDA settings—namely single-source, multi-source, and partial-set—verify that the proposed method attains performance that is highly competitive against leading data-dependent methods. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

author: Roberts
title: Enhancing Deep Neural Network Interpretability through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Across a broad range of tasks—including speech recognition, computer vision, and language modeling—Deep Neural Networks have delivered tremendous results. Yet strong accuracy by itself no longer meets the requirements of real-world deployment, since interpretability becomes essential in mission critical settings and situations that raise ethical concerns. Because these networks rely on complex models, explaining and reasoning about their predictions remains difficult, which stands in the way of continued advancement. We address this issue by employing the Knowledge Distillation technique to compress Deep Neural Networks into decision trees, thereby securing both interpretability and strong performance together. We cast the task as a multi-output regression problem, and our experiments show that, holding tree depth constant, the student model reaches markedly higher accuracy than vanilla decision trees, by roughly 1\% to 5\%. We carry out these experiments on the TensorFlow platform so that the approach scales to large datasets. As far as we are aware, this is the first work to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees for multi-class datasets.

author: Miller
title: Examining the Distillation of BERT-Based Rankers
abstract: State-of-the-art ranking systems for information retrieval have seen substantial gains thanks to deep language models like BERT that are pre-trained over large corpus. The complex matching signals between queries and passages become detectable to these models because of the knowledge they encode. Their adoption in practical search settings is nonetheless hindered by the heavy computation cost incurred at inference time. Whether and by what means the search-relevant knowledge held in BERT can be passed to a more compact ranker via distillation is the question we investigate here. According to our experiments, adopting an appropriate distillation procedure matters greatly: doing so yields speedups reaching nine times while the state-of-the-art performance is retained.

author: Hall
title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer for Federated Learning under Resource Constraints and Heterogeneous On-Device Models
abstract: By keeping on-device data decentralized, federated learning lets many distributed devices jointly train a common prediction model. A limitation of most existing methods is that they demand roughly equal local training burdens using on-device models of identical size and structure, an assumption that blocks resource-constrained devices from joining. Motivated by the abundance and diversity of today's devices, this paper introduces a novel federated learning framework that accommodates heterogeneous on-device models via zero-shot knowledge transfer. Under the proposed method, each device selects its on-device model according to the resources available to it. Knowledge transfer among these heterogeneous on-device models is accomplished through a zero-shot distillation scheme that imposes no requirement on private on-device data, in contrast to some earlier work that relies on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. To enable resource-constrained devices to take part, the heavy distillation computation is delegated to the server, where a generator is trained adversarially against the ensemble formed from the gathered on-device models. The resulting distilled central knowledge is returned as the matching on-device model parameters, which devices can readily incorporate. Comprehensive experiments confirm that the proposed method is both effective and robust with respect to on-device knowledge agnosticism, on-device model heterogeneity, and further demanding federated learning conditions, including heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

author: Garcia
title: Knowledge Distillation for the Compression of Visual-linguistic Models
abstract: While pre-training methods for visual-linguistic (VL) representations have advanced impressively, the goal of obtaining a compact VL model has attracted little attention. Here we investigate how knowledge distillation (KD) can be applied to shrink a large transformer-based VL model down to a small VL model. A key difficulty stems from the fact that the Teacher and the Student rely on different detectors, so their extracted regional visual tokens are inconsistent, which in turn misaligns the hidden representations and the attention distributions. Our remedy is to adapt and retrain the Teacher so that it consumes the identical region proposals produced by the Student's detector, whereas the features continue to come from the Teacher's own object detector. Once the network inputs match, this adapted Teacher can pass knowledge along via the intermediate representations. Concretely, an mean square error loss is employed to reproduce the attention distribution within the transformer block, and we introduce a token-wise noise contrastive loss that aligns the hidden state by contrasting against negative representations kept in a sample queue. Through this design, the proposed distillation yields substantial gains for small VL models on visual question answering and image captioning. On COCO captioning it attains a CIDEr score of 120.8, exceeding the non-distilled version by 5.1; on VQA 2.0 it achieves 69.8 accuracy, a 0.8 gain over the baseline. A broad set of experiments and ablations verifies that VL distillation is effective during both the fine-tuning and pre-training stages.

author: Ramirez
title: Refining Targets Progressively for Self-Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A broad range of regularization techniques—such as constraining the function space, adding randomness throughout training, or expanding the dataset—have led to considerable gains in how well deep neural networks generalize. Here we introduce a straightforward but effective regularization approach, the proposed method, in which a model progressively distills its own knowledge so as to soften the hard targets (that is, one-hot vectors) over the course of training. This process fits naturally into the framework of knowledge distillation, where the student takes on the role of teacher for itself. Concretely, the targets are updated adaptively by blending the ground-truth labels with the model's own earlier predictions. We demonstrate that, by rescaling gradients based on how hard examples are to classify, the approach yields an effect resembling hard example mining. Any supervised learning task involving hard targets can benefit from the method, which pairs readily with existing regularization strategies to boost generalization even further. Beyond improved accuracy, we confirm that it delivers high-quality confidence estimates with respect to both calibration and ordinal ranking. Across three distinct tasks—image classification, object detection, and machine translation—comprehensive experiments show that our method reliably outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines. The code can be found at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Distillation via Inexpensive Convolutions for Compact Networks
abstract: Deploying contemporary neural networks under tight memory budgets is a common goal among practitioners, yet adaptable techniques for shrinking memory footprints remain immature, and their trade-offs are poorly understood. To address memory reduction, we introduce structural model distillation, whose approach yields a student architecture obtained through a straightforward modification of the teacher architecture: neither architectural redesign nor new hyperparameters are required, since the existing ones carry over. Applying attention transfer, we distill residual networks across four benchmark datasets and report Pareto curves/tables that characterize the accuracy-memory trade-off. Our results demonstrate that considerable reductions in memory incur only minimal accuracy degradation, and we verify that a student trained through distillation outperforms the identical student architecture trained directly on the data.

author: Diaz
title: A Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation Approach to Model Compression for Web Question Answering Systems
abstract: In the domain of question answering, models built through deep pre-training followed by fine-tuning, including BERT and OpenAI GPT, have shown outstanding performance. Their enormous parameter counts, however, render inference extremely slow. Deploying such elaborate models within actual business settings therefore constitutes a difficult yet real-world problem. Compressing models typically causes information loss along the way, so the resulting compact models tend to fall short of their originals. We address this issue with the proposed method, a two-stage multi-teacher knowledge distillation technique designed for web Question Answering systems. The first stage introduces a generic Q&A distillation task used to pre-train the student model; the second stage applies multi-teacher knowledge distillation to fine-tune this pre-trained student model on downstream tasks (such as the Web Q&A task and the MNLI, SNLI, and RTE tasks from GLUE). This procedure curbs the overfitting bias present in single teacher models and conveys more general knowledge into the student model. According to our experiments, the approach considerably surpasses the baseline methods, can even match the performance of the original teacher models, and delivers a marked acceleration of model inference.

author: Wood
title: A Statistical View on Identifying Effective Data Augmentation for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A widely applicable strategy for training neural networks, knowledge distillation (KD) leverages a teacher model to supervise a student model. Most prior research has approached KD by focusing on the network output—for instance, by crafting improved KD loss functions—whereas the input side has drawn comparatively little attention. In particular, how KD relates to data augmentation (DA) remains poorly understood. Here we pose the following questions: what characterizes a "good" DA in the context of KD, and why are certain DA schemes such as CutMix intrinsically far more effective than alternatives? Approaching the problem statistically, our analysis indicates that an effective DA scheme ought to lower the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. We then propose a usable metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), and empirically confirm its validity. Beyond this theoretical account, we also put forward a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, referred to here as the proposed method, which builds upon CutMix. A broad range of experiments backs up our assertions and shows that substantial performance improvements can be obtained simply through the adoption of a superior DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

author: Clark
title: Distillation via Collaboration for Universal Style Transfer at Ultra-Resolution
abstract: To perform universal style transfer, methods commonly draw on the expressive representations of deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures such as VGG-19 that have been pre-trained over extensive image sets. Although such approaches work well, their large model size makes them difficult to deploy on ultra-resolution images under constrained memory budgets. Here we introduce a knowledge distillation technique, the proposed method, tailored to encoder-decoder neural style transfer with the goal of trimming the convolutional filters. Our central observation is that encoder-decoder pairs form a uniquely collaborative relationship, and we treat this as a novel form of knowledge for style transfer models. In addition, because the feature sizes fail to align during this collaborative distillation, we propose a linear embedding loss that guides the student network toward learning a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Across a range of universal style transfer frameworks (WCT and AdaIN), thorough experiments confirm that our approach remains effective even after shrinking the model by a factor of 15.5. Notably, using the compressed WCT models, we accomplish, for the first time, universal style transfer at ultra-resolution (exceeding 40 megapixels) on a single 12GB GPU. Additional tests on an optimization-based stylization setup demonstrate that our algorithm generalizes to distinct stylization paradigms. We release our code and trained models at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

author: Adams
title: Examining Deep Learning Heuristics More Carefully: Warmup, Learning Rate Restarts, and Distillation
abstract: Heuristics like normalization layers, skip connections, knowledge distillation, and learning rate schedules have markedly improved both how quickly widely used deep learning models converge and the quality they ultimately reach. Because a theoretical basis is lacking, understanding of training dynamics and deep learning landscapes may be advanced by controlled experiments designed to account for why these strategies work. The tools that current empirical studies depend on, namely linear interpolation and dimensionality-reduction visualizations, each come with drawbacks. We instead reexamine these heuristics using recently introduced techniques for analyzing representations and loss surfaces, specifically canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and mode connectivity, and we put forward conjectures about why the heuristics succeed. Concretely, we investigate knowledge distillation together with the (cosine) restart and warmup learning rate heuristics by means of CCA and mode connectivity. What our empirical study indicates is: (a) the explanations commonly given for why cosine annealing works are not borne out in practice; (b) that learning rate warmup functions by keeping the deeper layers from producing instability during training; and (c) that the hidden knowledge transferred from the teacher is delivered mainly to the deeper layers.

author: Zuniga
title: Scaling up distributed neural network training via online distillation
abstract: When combined with nearly any underlying model, methods like distillation and ensembling offer the prospect of better model quality. Yet these approaches prove difficult to deploy in industrial contexts, because ensembles raise the cost at test time and distillation makes the training pipeline more complex. Here we investigate a form of distillation that is comparatively easy to apply, since it avoids both an intricate multi-stage procedure and a large number of new hyperparameters. As a first claim, we argue that online distillation lets us exploit additional parallelism so that very large datasets can be fit roughly twice as quickly. What matters is that training can still be accelerated even beyond the point where extra parallelism no longer helps either synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. When two neural networks are each trained on non-overlapping portions of the data, they can exchange knowledge by pushing each model toward agreement with the predictions the other one would produce. Because those predictions may be drawn from an outdated copy of the other model, they can be computed safely from weights that are transmitted only infrequently. Our second claim holds that online distillation offers a cost-effective route to making a model's precise predictions substantially more reproducible. We back these claims with experiments on ImageNet, the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, and the largest dataset employed for neural language modeling so far, which draws on the Common Crawl repository of web data and comprises $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens.

author: Wong
title: Leveraging Dark Knowledge for Domain Generalization via a Regularized Knowledge Distillation Approach
abstract: A key obstacle to deploying convolutional neural networks in practice is their tendency to generalize poorly when representative and abundant data are not available, even though such networks see broad use across many tasks. To address this, we introduce a training approach that is easy to implement, works out of the box, and proves effective; it rests on a knowledge distillation framework and incorporates a gradient filter as a new regularization term. Our observation is that the mapping becomes easier to learn thanks to both the gradient filter we introduce and the ``richer dark knowledge" supplied by the teacher network, which in turn boosts how well the model generalizes. Through extensive experiments spanning image classification, segmentation, and reinforcement learning, and through comparisons against current state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques, we demonstrate that the proposed method markedly enhances the generalization capability of deep neural networks. Finally, to shed light on why our method improves the generalization capability of deep neural networks, we introduce two metrics for analyzing it.

author: Lynch
title: A Fresh Look at Knowledge Distillation Through the Lens of Label Smoothing Regularization
abstract: The goal of Knowledge Distillation (KD) is to transfer the knowledge held by a bulky teacher model over to a compact student model. The effectiveness of this transfer is usually credited to the special information about inter-category similarities that the teacher model supplies, and for this reason it is customary in practice to employ only powerful teacher models when instructing weaker students. Here we question this widely held assumption on the basis of the following empirical findings: 1) not only can the teacher benefit the student, as is commonly recognized, but the student can also markedly improve the teacher when the KD process is run in reverse; 2) a badly trained teacher whose accuracy falls well below that of the student is nonetheless able to boost the student substantially. To account for these findings, we present a theoretical study of how KD relates to label smoothing regularization. Our proofs establish that 1) KD amounts to a learned form of label smoothing regularization, and 2) label smoothing regularization supplies a virtual teacher model for KD. On this basis, we contend that the effectiveness of KD stems not solely from the teacher's category-similarity information, but also from the regularization brought by soft targets, a factor that is at least as, or even more, significant. Building on these findings, we go on to introduce a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation framework, in which a student model is trained either from its own output or from a manually designed regularization distribution. The proposed method reaches performance on par with standard KD driven by a stronger teacher, making it a good fit for situations where no more capable teacher model can be obtained. At the same time, the proposed method is general and can be applied directly to the training of deep neural networks. Incurring no additional computational overhead, it delivers gains of as much as 0.65\% on ImageNet relative to established baseline models, outperforming label smoothing regularization.

author: Jackson
title: Mutual Contrastive Learning for Online Knowledge Distillation in Visual Recognition Tasks
abstract: In teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD), the goal is to jointly train a set of student models that cooperatively share knowledge with one another. Current online KD techniques, while attaining strong results, tend to treat class probabilities as the primary knowledge type and overlook the useful information carried by feature representations. To address this, we introduce the proposed method for online KD. Its central concept is to exchange and mutually transfer contrastive distributions across a group of networks in an online fashion. By combining embedding information from different networks, the proposed method maximizes the lower bound on the mutual information shared between any pair of networks. As a result, every network acquires supplementary contrastive knowledge from its peers, which yields improved feature representations and consequently enhances performance on visual recognition tasks. We further generalize this approach past the final layer to intermediate layers, employing an adaptive layer-matching mechanism that is optimized via meta-optimization. Across image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks, our experiments demonstrate that the layer-wise variant delivers consistent gains over state-of-the-art online KD approaches. This advantage confirms that the layer-wise formulation steers networks toward generating superior feature representations. The code is released publicly at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial Distillation Without Access to Data
abstract: Over recent years, Knowledge Distillation (KD) has advanced considerably and emerged as a widely adopted approach for transferring knowledge and compressing models. A limitation shared by nearly every existing KD algorithm, however, is their data-driven nature: they depend on substantial quantities of the original training data or some surrogate data, resources that real-world settings frequently do not provide. We take on this difficult setting here, presenting a new adversarial distillation scheme that produces a compact student model while requiring no real-world data whatsoever. Our formulation defines a model discrepancy that numerically captures how far apart the student and teacher models are, and derives from it an upper bound amenable to optimization. Within this framework, the teacher and the student together serve as the discriminator that shrinks the discrepancy, while a generator, in adversarial fashion, synthesizes certain "hard samples" that widen it. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that the proposed data-free method attains performance on par with methods that are data-driven. Even more notably, the approach transfers directly to semantic segmentation—a task more intricate than classification—where it reaches state-of-the-art results. Pretrained models and code can be found at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

author: Martin
title: Transferring BERT's Knowledge into Sequence-to-Sequence ASR via Distillation
abstract: In automatic speech recognition (ASR), attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have shown encouraging outcomes. A limitation, though, is that decoding proceeds from left to right, leaving the rightward context unavailable to these models. To make use of context on both sides, we bring BERT into seq2seq ASR as an external language model by way of knowledge distillation. The approach we propose has BERT produce soft labels that steer how the seq2seq ASR is trained. We additionally feed BERT with context that extends past the utterance being processed. Our experiments on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) demonstrate that the seq2seq baseline is substantially improved by our method in terms of ASR performance. When knowledge distillation draws on BERT, it surpasses distillation from a transformer LM restricted to left context. The benefit of drawing on context outside the current utterance is likewise confirmed. Compared with alternative ways of applying an LM, including n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, our method performs better and incurs no additional inference cost.

author: Gray
title: Boosting Feature Distillation through an Ensemble of Projectors
abstract: While earlier approaches to feature distillation within knowledge distillation have concentrated their efforts on how loss functions are constructed and which distilled layers to pick, the role played by the feature projector connecting the student and the teacher has received comparatively little attention. Here, we begin by examining, with supporting empirical evidence, a likely account of how the projector operates, and we subsequently introduce a novel feature distillation method that relies on an ensemble of projectors to push performance still higher. Our finding is that the student network gains from having a projector, and this holds true even when the feature dimensions match between the student and the teacher. When a student backbone is trained in the absence of a projector, the situation resembles multi-task learning: the network must simultaneously carry out discriminative feature extraction for classification and, for the sake of distillation, feature matching against the teacher. We put forward the hypothesis—and confirm it empirically—that a student lacking a projector is prone to overfitting the teacher's feature distributions, notwithstanding differences in architecture and in weight initialization. As a consequence, the quality of the student's deep features, which are ultimately relied upon for classification, deteriorates. Introducing a projector, by contrast, separates these two learning tasks, allowing the student network to concentrate more effectively on its principal feature extraction objective while continuing to draw on teacher features as guidance by way of the projector. Encouraged by this beneficial role of the projector in feature distillation, we advance an ensemble of projectors as a means of further raising the quality of student features. Experiments spanning several datasets and a range of teacher-student pairs demonstrate that the proposed method is effective.

author: Mayo
title: Reconsidering Soft Labels in Knowledge Distillation Through the Lens of the Bias-Variance Tradeoff
