abstract: To transfer the capabilities of a well-trained network, or a collection of such networks acting jointly as the teacher, knowledge distillation guides how a student network is trained. In this scheme, the teacher's predictions become soft labels that supervise the learning of the new network. It was recently shown \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} that softening the labels has an interesting effect: it functions as an effective regularizer for the student network. Regularization, viewed from statistical learning theory, is meant to lower the variance, yet it remains unclear how both bias and variance evolve when training relies on soft labels. Here we study the bias-variance tradeoff that distillation with soft labels introduces. In particular, we find that over the course of training this tradeoff differs from one sample to another. Moreover, keeping the distillation temperature fixed, we notice that distillation performance declines as the count of certain samples grows; we call these regularization samples because they push bias upward while pulling variance downward. However, our experiments show that discarding regularization samples entirely likewise harms distillation performance. Motivated by these findings, we introduce weighted soft labels, which enable the network to cope adaptively with the per-sample bias-variance tradeoff. Tests on standard evaluation benchmarks confirm that the proposed method works. Our code can be found at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

author: Bowman
title: Compact Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations via Distillation
abstract: The quality of speech representations has seen remarkable gains thanks to progress in self-supervision. Bringing leading embedding models onto devices, however, remains difficult because such models are seldom released publicly and carry heavy resource demands. To tackle these obstacles, we make available a set of compact paralinguistic speech models whose performance sits close to the leading edge. We rely on knowledge distillation, using exclusively public data to distill our models. After examining a range of architectures, we assess them carefully against the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. At under 15% of the source model's size (314MB against 2.2GB), our biggest distilled model reaches above 96% of the accuracy on 6 of the 7 tasks while being trained with just 6.5% of the data. Our most compact model, at 1% of the size (22MB), still exceeds 90% of the accuracy on 6 of the 7 tasks. On 6 of the 7 tasks our models beat the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model, and even our smallest one surpasses the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks while occupying only 7% of the size.

author: Hawkins
title: An Efficient Knowledge Distillation Approach for Visual Recognition
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is widely acknowledged as a valuable technique across numerous visual applications, including supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning. Nevertheless, the standard KD pipeline suffers from a critical limitation: most of its computational cost stems from repeatedly forwarding inputs through the enormous teacher networks, rendering the whole training process expensive and slow. A recent method, ReLabel, addresses this by producing a label map spanning the full image; throughout training, region-level labels for cropped patches are obtained via RoI aligning on this precomputed full label map, so that supervision can be generated efficiently without traversing the teachers repeatedly. Yet because the KD teachers originate from standard multi-crop training, this scheme suffers numerous discrepancies between the region-level label and the global label-map, which degrades performance. Here we introduce the proposed method, which mirrors the distillation training stage and produces soft labels through the multi-crop KD strategy, achieving faster training than ReLabel by avoiding post-processing steps like RoI align and softmax operations. During data loading, when multi-crop is applied within the same image, the proposed method runs even faster than the conventional image classification pipeline. Using ResNet-50 on ImageNet-1K, we reach 79.8%, which surpasses ReLabel by roughly 1.0% at higher speed. We further demonstrate that the proposed method offers an efficiency benefit on the self-supervised learning task. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

author: Cohen
title: Fusing Teacher Layers via Attention for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: As a strategy for both training and compression, knowledge distillation pairs two neural networks—a teacher and a student—throughout the training process. Serving as a reliable predictor, the teacher provides outputs that the student attempts to reproduce. To obtain compression while still yielding strong results, the student is typically given a lighter architecture. Under this arrangement, only the final predictions are subject to distillation, even though supervision from the teacher over internal components could also help the student. This observation led us to investigate distilling from intermediate layers. Because student and teacher layers may lack a one-to-one correspondence, prior approaches drop certain teacher layers and distill from only a portion of them. Such omission has a direct negative effect on quality; therefore, we put forward a combinatorial method built on attention. By merging information across the teacher and weighing the importance of each layer, the proposed method carries out distillation between the student's layers and the aggregated teacher layers. Applying this approach, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into versions with 6, 4, and 2 layers, which we assessed on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). The experiments demonstrate that our combinatorial method surpasses the other available techniques.

author: Cameron
title: Compact Models Benefit From Broad Reading: Why Pre-training Small Networks Matters
abstract: Progress in natural language representations has gone hand in hand with costly, large models that exploit enormous quantities of general-domain text via self-supervised pre-training. Because deploying these models on down-stream tasks is expensive, prior work has introduced various schemes for compressing pre-trained language representations (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). Yet the plain baseline of simply pre-training and then fine-tuning compact models has, surprisingly, received little attention. Here we begin by demonstrating that, even for smaller architectures, pre-training still matters, and that fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can rival the more sophisticated approaches from concurrent work. Building on these pre-trained compact models, we next investigate moving task knowledge from large fine-tuned models using conventional knowledge distillation. This yields a straightforward but effective and broadly applicable procedure, the proposed method, which delivers additional gains. With comprehensive experiments, we examine more broadly how pre-training and distillation interact along two variables that have been under-studied: the size of the model and the characteristics of the unlabeled task data. A striking finding is that these produce a compound effect even when applied one after another to the very same data. To speed up subsequent research, we will publicly release our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models.

author: Parsons
title: A Curriculum Learning Approach to Distillation for Dense Retrieval
abstract: Distilling ranking knowledge out of a pre-existing base re-ranking model has recently been demonstrated as a route toward stronger dense retrieval models. We introduce here a general optimization framework grounded in curriculum learning that regulates how hard the training data generated by the re-ranking (teacher) model becomes. Through repeated iterations, the proposed method trains the dense retrieval (student) model while gradually raising the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data it receives. Specifically, the student model is first exposed to coarse-grained preference pairs among documents drawn from the teacher's ranking, and the requirements then advance step by step toward finer-grained pairwise ordering of documents. For our experiments, a straightforward implementation of the framework is used to improve two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Evaluations across three public passage retrieval datasets confirm that the proposed framework is effective.

author: Perez
title: Reborn Multi-Task Networks: Distilling Single-Task Knowledge for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: Matching, let alone exceeding, the performance of single-task counterparts remains a difficult goal when training multi-task neural networks. As a remedy, we introduce a knowledge distillation scheme in which a multi-task model learns from single-task teachers. This procedure is augmented with teacher annealing, a new technique that shifts the model progressively away from distillation and toward supervised learning, thereby enabling the multi-task model to outperform the single-task teachers that guided it. To assess the approach, we perform multi-task fine-tuning of BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Relative to conventional single-task and multi-task training, our method yields consistent gains.

author: Stewart
title: Privacy-Preserving Model Compression through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Running capable deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices has become necessary as intelligent mobile applications grow rapidly in popularity. Yet the impressive accuracy of DNNs is well known to depend on models of ever-greater complexity, whose computational demands vastly exceed what mobile hardware can supply. Compounding this, the construction of these elaborate DNN models requires app service providers to gather and process substantial amounts of user data that hold sensitive information. Placing such models directly onto public mobile devices therefore carries unacceptable privacy risk. So that on-device deep learning can be enjoyed free of these capacity and privacy limitations, we introduce a framework for private model compression. Within the knowledge distillation paradigm, we combine hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to produce a lightweight, rapid neural network. To guarantee differential privacy, the knowledge extracted from the bulky model is adaptively bounded and deliberately perturbed. We additionally introduce a refined scheme for selecting query samples that lowers the query count while keeping the privacy loss in check. Both a set of empirical studies and a deployment on an Android mobile device demonstrate that the proposed method achieves efficient compression of unwieldy models along with a robust privacy guarantee. As an illustration, under a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy guarantee on SVHN, the compact model produced by the proposed method attains a 20$\times$ compression ratio and a 19$\times$ speed-up while sacrificing only 0.97% accuracy.

author: Adams
title: Revisiting the Supposed Conflict Between Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Investigation
abstract: A claim raised recently holds that label smoothing cannot coexist with knowledge distillation, and the goal of this study is to examine that claim empirically. Our starting point explains the reasoning behind the alleged conflict, namely the notion that label smoothing wipes out the relative information carried in teacher logits. We then draw a fresh link describing the way label smoothing reshapes the distributions across classes that are semantically similar as well as those that differ. Building on this, we introduce a metric that quantifies, for a given sample's representation, how much information has been eliminated. Through extensive analyses, visualizations, and thorough experiments spanning Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation, we expose the partial and flawed nature of the incompatibility argument. To close, we discuss in general terms the various settings under which label smoothing does in fact cease to be beneficial. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

author: Clark
title: Knowledge Distillation as a Path Toward Model Agnostic Federated Learning
abstract: Could a universal API be constructed to let a spontaneously assembled set of data-holders (agents) jointly carry out federated learning? For this to work, the API would have to remain model-agnostic, meaning it presumes nothing regarding which model architecture each agent employs, and it must also function without access to representative public data. The natural instrument for building such protocols is knowledge distillation (KD). Yet we demonstrate, somewhat unexpectedly, that the most intuitive KD-based federated learning protocols yield weak results. We examine this phenomenon by introducing a fresh theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, that accounts for heterogeneity in both models and data. According to our analysis, the drop in performance stems chiefly from an inherent shortcoming of knowledge distillation when data heterogeneity is present. To further test the framework, we study and construct additional KD-based protocols. When run on real world experiments with neural networks, their performance—while still not satisfactory—aligns tightly with what our theory anticipates.

author: Hahn
title: A General Object Detector Distillation Framework Based on the Pearson Correlation Coefficient
abstract: To produce lightweight object detection models, knowledge distillation (KD) has become a common approach. Yet how distillation should proceed across heterogeneous detectors remains under-explored. Through empirical study, we observe that a student can benefit from superior FPN features supplied by a heterogeneous teacher detector, even when the two disagree in their detection heads and label assignments. Nevertheless, distilling detectors by aligning feature maps directly gives rise to two difficulties. To begin with, when the teacher and the student differ in feature magnitude, the student may be subjected to excessively rigid constraints. In addition, those FPN stages and channels in which the teacher exhibits large feature magnitude tend to dominate the gradient of the distillation loss, thereby drowning out the contribution of other features during KD and bringing in substantial noise. As a remedy for these problems, we suggest imitating features via the Pearson Correlation Coefficient, which emphasizes the relational information carried by the teacher while easing constraints tied to feature magnitude. Applicable to both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs, our method consistently surpasses prior detection KD approaches, and it also converges more quickly. Using a strong MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS reach 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, exceeding the baseline by 4.1% and 4.8%, respectively.

author: Walter
title: Distilling Knowledge When the Teacher Is More Powerful
abstract: Current knowledge distillation techniques are typically evaluated in baseline configurations, in which neither the teacher models nor the training strategies match the strength and competitiveness of state-of-the-art approaches; departing from this, we introduce the proposed method for improved distillation from a stronger teacher. Through experiments, we observe that the gap between what the student predicts and what a stronger teacher predicts tends to grow considerably larger. Consequently, forcing predictions to align exactly via KL divergence interferes with training and leaves existing methods underperforming. We demonstrate here that it is enough to merely maintain the relationships among the predictions of teacher and student, and we introduce a correlation-based loss that explicitly extracts the underlying inter-class relations from the teacher. Furthermore, since distinct instances carry distinct degrees of semantic similarity to each class, we broaden this relational alignment to the intra-class level as well. Being both simple and practical, our approach, as shown by comprehensive experiments, generalizes effectively across diverse architectures, model sizes, and training strategies, and reliably reaches state-of-the-art results on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

author: Edwards
title: Privacy Protection for Federated Learning via Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
abstract: In the Federated Learning (FL) paradigm, a shared central model is trained cooperatively by local nodes, yet the underlying training data stays distributed across those nodes. To cope with skewed data distributions, current FL approaches generally rely on exchanging model parameters or on co-distillation. Such approaches, though, are constrained by communication bottlenecks and, still more critically, by the danger of leaking private information. Here we design a method within an FL framework that is both communication efficient and privacy preserving, drawing on one-shot offline knowledge distillation with public data that is unlabeled and cross-domain. Local models are trained to completion, and we combine their predictions into an ensemble that is quantized and noised, which strengthens privacy guarantees while leaving accuracy intact. Through comprehensive experiments spanning image classification and text classification, we demonstrate that our privacy-preserving approach surpasses baseline FL algorithms, delivering better accuracy alongside greater communication efficiency.

author: Rios
title: Enhancing Neural Topic Models through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: To help interpret extensive collections of documents, topic models frequently serve to surface topics that people can readily understand. Drawing on knowledge distillation, we merge the strongest qualities of pretrained transformers with those of probabilistic topic models. Because our approach is modular, it can be paired with essentially any neural topic model to raise topic quality; we illustrate this with two models whose architectures differ substantially, reaching state-of-the-art topic coherence. Beyond the aggregate gains across all estimated topics that are typically reported, we further establish that this flexible framework yields improvements when aligned topics are compared directly against one another.

author: Foster
title: Distilling Knowledge from Teacher Ensembles for CTR Prediction
abstract: Across numerous industrial deployments, models grounded in deep learning have lately received considerable attention for click-through rate (CTR) prediction, where they have raised the accuracy of predictions. Yet the bulk of existing efforts concentrate on designing intricate network architectures that more effectively capture dynamic user behaviors and sophisticated feature interactions. Such growth in model complexity risks slowing online inference and impeding deployment in real-time settings. Our contribution instead pursues a fresh training strategy rooted in knowledge distillation (KD), a teacher-student learning framework through which knowledge acquired by a teacher model is passed to a student model. Beyond letting us reduce the student model to a plain vanilla DNN, the KD strategy delivers notable accuracy gains relative to state-of-the-art teacher models. Encouraged by these gains, we go on to investigate how a strong ensemble of teachers can drive more accurate training of the student model. To support ensembled CTR prediction, we further introduce several new techniques, among them teacher gating and early stopping governed by distillation loss. We carry out thorough experiments spanning three industrial datasets and contrasting our approach with 12 prior models. Results from offline evaluation as well as online A/B testing confirm that our KD-based training strategy is effective.

author: Rocha
title: Compressing Networks under Few-Shot Constraints through Interleaved Distillation
abstract: To produce compact deep neural networks, model compression has become a common practice. Yet the accuracy of most leading techniques hinges on fine-tuning with ample training data, a requirement that privacy and security concerns may render impractical. Balancing performance against privacy, this work studies few shot network compression, asking whether a network can be compressed with barely any loss in performance when only a handful of samples per class are on hand. The central difficulty of few shot network compression stems from large estimation errors relative to the original network at inference time, because so few training instances make the compressed network prone to over-fitting. Layer by layer, these estimation errors can spread and build up, ultimately degrading what the network outputs. We tackle this by introducing the proposed method, a fresh layer-wise knowledge distillation scheme. Interweaving the hidden layers of the teacher and student network curbs the estimation errors that otherwise accumulate across layers. This design constitutes a general framework that fits well with widespread network compression methods, pruning among them. Across benchmark datasets, thorough experiments show that the approach markedly raises the student network's accuracy in the regime where training instances are scarce.

author: Ellis
title: Distilling Representation Knowledge in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: To improve resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs), knowledge distillation offers a learning paradigm in which more expressive but unwieldy teacher models guide the training. Earlier distillation approaches for GNNs introduced the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which aligns edge-defined local structural relationships between the node embeddings of the teacher and the student. Because real-world graphs frequently harbor noisy edges and hidden interactions, this work investigates whether a more effective distillation target for GNNs might instead retain the global topology of the teacher's graph embedding. Our contribution is a method built on contrastive learning that implicitly maintains global topology by mapping the student node embeddings toward the teacher's within a shared representation space. We also present a broadened suite of benchmarks drawn from large-scale real-world datasets, in which the teacher–student GNN performance gap is non-negligible. Across 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures and 4 datasets, experiments demonstrate that the proposed method reliably enhances both robustness and performance of lightweight GNNs, surpassing LSP (along with a variant of LSP that preserves global structure) and baselines adapted from 2D computer vision. Examining the representational similarity between the teacher and student embedding spaces shows that the proposed method strikes a balance in retaining local and global relationships, whereas structure preserving methods excel at only one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

author: Baker
title: Reviving Low-Frequency Words: Fully Exploiting Parallel Data for Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: To generate synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models, knowledge distillation (KD) is a standard technique. A mismatch in low-frequency words nevertheless arises between the original data and its distilled counterpart, which yields a higher rate of mistakes when low-frequency words are predicted. We address this issue by feeding the raw data directly into NAT through the use of pretraining. Our examination of directed alignments revealed that, while KD aligns low-frequency source words to targets in a more deterministic fashion, it does not produce enough alignments running from target to source for low-frequency words. In light of this, we introduce reverse KD to revive additional alignments covering low-frequency target words. So that both authentic and synthetic data are used to their fullest, we merge these complementary techniques into a fresh training strategy that further elevates NAT performance. Across two advanced architectures, we run experiments on five translation benchmarks. The findings show that our proposed approach lowers translation errors involving low-frequency words and thereby improves translation quality in a substantial and universal manner. Notably, on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets our approach attains 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points, respectively. We release our code, data, and trained models at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

author: Wright
title: Comprehensive Video Scene Understanding via Distilled Semantics
abstract: For autonomous systems, perceiving the entire environment is of critical importance. Because ground truth annotations are especially difficult to obtain for depth and optical flow, it is notable that recent studies have demonstrated deep neural networks capable of inferring geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) directly from a monocular video, requiring no explicit supervision from such annotations. Here, we advance toward holistic scene understanding using monocular cameras: jointly with depth and motion, we also learn semantics, whose supervision comes from a pre-trained network that distills proxy ground truth images. These three tasks are tackled together through two contributions: first, a training protocol that combines self-supervision with knowledge distillation; second, a lightweight network architecture that permits efficient scene understanding across both energy-intensive GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. Our extensive evaluation of the framework demonstrates that it achieves state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow, and motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Knowledge Distillation in Federated Settings
abstract: Rather than exposing their local raw data, workers in distributed learning frameworks frequently share model parameters among themselves. Federated learning stands out as a leading instance, where the gradients or weights of every neural network model are passed around. This approach, though, grows prohibitively expensive when communication resources are scarce, especially for today's deep neural networks that carry enormous numbers of model parameters. Federated distillation (FD) addresses this concern as an attractive distributed learning alternative, since it communicates only the model outputs, which typically have far smaller dimensions than the model sizes (for instance, the 10 labels of the MNIST dataset). This chapter aims to build a thorough grasp of FD alongside evidence of both its efficiency in communication and its relevance across many tasks. Accordingly, the opening portion sheds light on how FD works by contributing a new asymptotic analysis of its two foundational algorithms, knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), drawing on neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. The middle portion then develops a baseline FD implementation for a classification task and shows how it fares in accuracy and communication efficiency relative to FL. Finally, to establish that FD carries over to diverse distributed learning tasks and environments, the closing portion offers two chosen applications: FD across asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels, and FD applied to reinforcement learning.

author: Baker
title: Consolidating Heterogeneous Classifiers via Distillation
abstract: Here we address how to consolidate, into one classifier, the knowledge held by several classifiers that vary in their architectures and their target classes, relying solely on a generic pool of unlabelled data. We refer to this task as the consolidation of heterogeneous classifiers. Real-world settings motivate the task: consider data drawn from several sources that, perhaps because of privacy concerns, are prohibited from exchanging their data, so that only models trained in private may be shared. Furthermore, depending on what data is available at a given source, that source might lack the samples needed to cover every class, and differing computational budgets may prevent sources from adopting an identical classification model. Our answer to this task is a generalisation of knowledge distillation that fuses such heterogeneous classifiers. We establish a probabilistic link between what these classifiers output and the probability across the full set of classes. Building on that link, we introduce two families of techniques, one grounded in cross-entropy minimisation and the other in matrix factorisation, both of which infer soft labels spanning all classes from unlabelled examples; these soft labels then substitute for ground truth labels when training the consolidated classifier. Across thorough experiments on the ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets, the proposed methods markedly surpass a naive distillation baseline and reach accuracy nearly matching that of classifiers trained centrally under full supervision.

author: Richards
title: Combining Knowledge Distillation with Generative Adversarial Networks for Text Generation
abstract: Across a range of NLP tasks—among them language modeling, machine translation, and text summarization—text generation remains a topic of considerable importance. In the field of computer vision, generative adversarial networks (GANs) have delivered impressive results for producing high quality images, and this success has more recently drawn substantial attention within the NLP community. Because text is discrete, however, replicating comparable outcomes for NLP is expected to be harder. This paper presents an approach that leverages knowledge distillation as a way to make the GAN framework work well for text generation. We show that autoencoders (AEs) are able to yield continuous, smooth sentence representations in which several words receive non-zero probabilities rather than a single one. By distilling such a representation, the generator is trained to produce comparable smooth representations. Validating the idea through several experiments over various datasets, we find that, relative to conventional GAN-based text generation methods that omit pre-training, the proposed approach achieves stronger results as measured by the BLEU score and the Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD).

author: Hurst
title: Compact yet High-Performing Ranking Models via Distillation for Recommendation
abstract: This work introduces a fresh approach to building ranking models—recommender systems among them—that combine efficiency with strong effectiveness. Prior work established that knowledge distillation (KD) delivers both qualities in image recognition. Here, we adapt KD to learning-to-rank settings through a technique we refer to as the proposed method. Concretely, a smaller student model is trained to rank documents/items by drawing on the training data together with guidance provided by a larger teacher model. Although the student model is more compact—which yields more efficient online inference—it attains ranking performance close to that of the large teacher model. Because it does not depend on any particular teacher or student ranking model, the proposed method remains flexible and orthogonal to those design choices. We also tackle the specific difficulties that arise when applying this idea to ranking problems. Using public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models, our experiments confirm that the proposed method meets its objectives: a student model trained with it occupies under half the size of the teacher model, yet reaches ranking performance on par with the teacher and far exceeding a student trained without the proposed method.

author: Ross
title: Distilling from Model Ensembles for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: A student network can be trained to reach higher performance by drawing on a more capable teacher network, an approach known as knowledge distillation. Because producing a translation through a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine consumes considerable time, reducing model size accelerates the operation. We show that the translation quality achieved by an ensemble, as well as by an oracle BLEU teacher network, can be conveyed into one NMT system. In addition, we report gains in translation obtained even when the teacher network shares identical architecture and dimensions with the student network. Since training the student model remains costly, we propose a data filtering scheme grounded in what the teacher model knows; this approach both accelerates training and yields improved translation quality. The methods we describe require no modification to the code and are readily reproducible on any NMT architecture in order to hasten decoding.

author: Robinson
title: Analyzing and Enhancing Lexical Choice for Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: To train non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models, knowledge distillation (KD) plays a critical role, since an autoregressive teacher model lowers the complexity of the raw data. Here, we provide empirical evidence that a byproduct of this training procedure is the transfer of lexical choice errors on low-frequency words from the teacher model into the NAT model. As a remedy, we suggest presenting the raw data to NAT models so that the beneficial information about low-frequency words—absent from the distilled data—can be recovered. Concretely, we add an auxiliary Kullback-Leibler divergence term that contrasts the lexical choice of the NAT model against the lexical choice captured within the raw data. Across a range of language pairs and model architectures, our experiments establish that the proposed approach is both effective and broadly applicable. Through extensive analyses, we substantiate the claim that the gains stem from fewer lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Notably, the proposed approach raises the SOTA NAT results to 27.8 BLEU points on WMT14 English-German and 33.8 BLEU points on WMT16 Romanian-English. We will make the source code available.

author: Bright
title: Distilled and Efficient Models for Deployable Lipreading
abstract: The revival of neural networks has driven considerable advances in lipreading. Attention in recent studies has focused on boosting accuracy through the search for optimal architectures or through better generalization. Nonetheless, a considerable distance remains between what these approaches offer and what is needed to deploy lipreading effectively in real-world settings. This paper introduces several contributions that substantially narrow this distance. To begin with, by applying self-distillation, we push the state-of-the-art on LRW and LRW-1000 well beyond prior results, reaching 88.5% and 46.6% respectively. Next, we introduce a set of architectural modifications, among them a new Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, which cuts the computational burden of the original—itself already fairly efficient—model down to a small fraction. Finally, we demonstrate that knowledge distillation serves as a highly effective means of restoring the accuracy of the lightweight models. The outcome is a family of models spanning various accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Our best lightweight models nonetheless match the current state-of-the-art, while achieving reductions of 8.2x in computational cost and 3.9x in parameter count, which we hope will make lipreading models deployable in practical applications.

author: Hicks
title: Adapting Knowledge: Learning How to Transfer Across Domains
abstract: When the statistical characteristics of test data diverge from those seen during training, domain adaptation becomes essential across numerous practical settings. Existing Deep Learning solutions for this problem require joint training over both source and target domain data, which makes them impractical when a model must accommodate many domains at once, or when a domain keeps shifting—consider spam detection, in which adversaries perpetually revise their methods. We address this shortcoming by introducing the proposed method, which carries Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) over into the domain adaptation setting. On a standard sentiment analysis benchmark, we demonstrate that a student model reaches state-of-the-art results for unsupervised domain adaptation drawing on multiple sources, because it leverages both the domain-specific expertise held by several teachers and how closely their domains resemble one another. Relying on domain similarity to judge trustworthiness falls short, however, when there is only a single teacher. For that case, we introduce a straightforward metric that tracks the teacher's accuracy in the target domain closely. By feeding the student model the high-confidence examples this metric picks out, we show that it attains state-of-the-art performance under the single-source scenario.

author: Williams
title: Adversarial Belief Matching for Data-Free Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Transferring knowledge from a sizable teacher network into a more compact student has become a common practice across contemporary deep learning applications. Yet, as datasets keep expanding and privacy rules tighten, access to the original training data of the teacher is frequently unavailable. In this work, we introduce a method that teaches a student to reproduce its teacher's predictions while relying on neither data nor metadata. The approach works by optimizing an adversarial generator that seeks out images where the student aligns poorly with the teacher, and these images are subsequently fed into the student's training. For straightforward datasets such as SVHN, the student we obtain provides a close approximation of its teacher, and on CIFAR10 our results surpass the prior state-of-the-art in few-shot distillation (using 100 images per class), even though no data is employed. Additionally, we put forward a metric that measures how closely teacher and student agree in belief near decision boundaries, and we find that our zero-shot student agrees with the teacher considerably more than a student distilled from real data does. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

author: Rodriguez
title: Distilling Graph Neural Network Knowledge and Surpassing It: A Powerful Knowledge Distillation Approach
abstract: Within machine learning, semi-supervised learning over graphs stands as a significant challenge. Classification approaches built on graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently achieved leading performance, outdoing conventional techniques like label propagation. Nevertheless, because these neural models rely on intricate architectures, their prediction procedures grow complicated and may fail to fully exploit the valuable prior knowledge present in the data, for instance the tendency of structurally correlated nodes to share a class. To tackle these concerns, this work introduces a framework grounded in knowledge distillation. The proposed method draws out the knowledge held by any trained GNN model, which serves as the teacher model, and transfers it into a carefully constructed student model. Two straightforward prediction mechanisms underpin the student model, namely label propagation and feature transformation, and these respectively retain prior knowledge of a structure-based and a feature-based nature by design. Concretely, the student model is formulated as a trainable combination of parameterized modules for label propagation and feature transformation. Consequently, the resulting student can draw on both the prior knowledge and the knowledge held by GNN teachers to yield more effective predictions. In addition, compared with GNNs, the prediction process of the learned student model is more interpretable. Across five public benchmark datasets, we run experiments using seven GNN models as teachers, namely GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP. The findings demonstrate that the learned student model reliably exceeds its matching teacher model, with average improvements ranging from 1.4% to 4.7%. Code and data can be found at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

author: Burton
title: Hardware-Aware Block Structured Pruning for Compact Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations
abstract: Across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, large-scale language models that have been pre-trained keep achieving strong accuracy. Their adoption, though, has been held back by constrained weight storage and computational throughput on hardware platforms, an issue that grows more pressing in the age of edge computing. We introduce here an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation built on a hardware-friendly form of block structured pruning. For the optimization, reweighted group Lasso is folded into the block-structured pruning scheme. Alongside a marked drop in both computation and weight storage, high compression rates are delivered by the proposed method. When evaluated over the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks across several models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT), the experiments reach as much as 5.0x with no or slight accuracy degradation on some task(s). Because it operates independently of existing compact pre-trained language models that rely on knowledge distillation, such as DistilBERT, the proposed method can push an additional 1.79x average compression rate beyond DistilBERT while incurring zero or minor accuracy degradation. The resulting compressed model lends itself well to deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

author: Conner
title: Transferring Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT to Lightweight Neural Networks via Distillation
abstract: Within research on natural language processing, the trend has been toward neural networks of ever greater depth and complexity. Deep language representation models such as BERT, ELMo, and GPT exemplify this recent direction. Such advances have fostered the belief that the shallower neural networks of earlier generations are no longer relevant for language understanding. Contrary to this view, we show in this work that basic, lightweight neural networks remain competitive even absent any modifications to the architecture, reliance on external training data, or use of extra input features. Our approach distills knowledge out of BERT, which represents the state of the art among language representation models, into a single-layer BiLSTM, along with a siamese variant designed for sentence-pair tasks. Evaluating on several datasets spanning sentiment classification, natural language inference, and paraphrasing, we obtain results on par with ELMo while requiring approximately 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times shorter inference time.

author: Henderson
title: From MLPs to Graph-Free Prediction: Boosting Simple Networks through Distillation
abstract: Widely used in graph machine learning, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) deliver strong performance across many node classification tasks. In industrial settings, however, they see limited adoption because data dependency creates scalability difficulties. Specifically, target-node inference in a GNN draws on neighbor nodes located several hops away, and retrieving those neighbors adds overhead that strains latency-constrained applications. Techniques already available for accelerating inference, such as quantization and pruning, cut Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations and thereby accelerate GNNs, yet the gains stay modest because the data dependency remains unaddressed. In contrast, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) carry no graph dependency and perform inference far more quickly than GNNs, although their node classification accuracy is typically lower. These opposing merits and shortcomings prompt us to unite MLPs and GNNs through knowledge distillation (KD). We demonstrate that distilling from a GNN can raise MLP performance substantially. Because the resulting distilled MLPs have no graph dependency during inference, we refer to them as graph-free networks. We report that, at competitive accuracy, the proposed distilled models infer 146X-273X faster than GNNs and 14X-27X faster than alternative acceleration approaches. Evaluated in a production scenario spanning transductive and inductive predictions over 7 datasets, the proposed method raises accuracy by 12.36% on average relative to standalone MLPs and equals GNNs on 6 of the 7 datasets. Thorough analysis clarifies the conditions and reasons behind the method reaching GNN-level accuracies and positions it as a convenient option for latency-constrained applications.

author: Brown
title: A Consolidated Framework for Compressing Visual Transformers
abstract: Recent interest has grown around vision transformers (ViTs), which are able to reach competitive performance—despite lacking tailored image operators like convolutions—provided they receive proper training over large-scale data. That said, ViTs still carry a computational burden that is often impractical, owing to their stacked multi-head self-attention modules among other components. While compressing convolutional neural networks has been studied extensively and met with widespread success, the compression of Vision Transformers is only beginning to attract attention, and prior efforts have addressed merely one or two facets of the problem. Here, we introduce a unified compression framework for ViTs that smoothly integrates three complementary techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. Under a distillation loss and subject to a budget constraint, we cast the problem as an end-to-end optimization that jointly learns the model weights, the per-layer pruning masks and ratios, and the skip configurations. We then tackle this optimization via the primal-dual algorithm. Using backbones such as DeiT and T2T-ViT, we run experiments on the ImageNet dataset across multiple ViT variants, and the proposed method reliably surpasses recent competing approaches. As an illustration, DeiT-Tiny can be reduced to half of its original FLOPs with virtually no drop in accuracy. Code is released at:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

author: James
title: Learning Resilient Cross-Modal Representations via Gradual Self-Distillation
abstract: Web-collected image captioning corpora exhibit noisy many-to-many correspondences that CLIP's vision-language training objective fails to handle well, a shortcoming that drives up its demand for both computation and data. We tackle this problem by proposing a training framework grounded in cross-modal contrastive learning, in which progressive self-distillation together with soft image-text alignments enables more efficient acquisition of robust representations from noisy inputs. In each minibatch, the model draws on its own knowledge to produce, on the fly, soft-alignment targets for a portion of the images and captions, and these targets subsequently drive the update of its parameters. Testing broadly on 14 benchmark datasets, we find that the proposed method reliably surpasses its CLIP counterpart across several regimes—namely (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval—while adding no computational overhead. When examined on an ImageNet-derived robustness test-bed, our approach delivers stronger effective robustness against natural distribution shifts than both CLIP and models trained on ImageNet. Finally, pretraining on datasets differing by two orders of magnitude in size indicates that the gains we obtain over CLIP tend to grow with the number of training examples.

author: Ferrell
title: Enhancing Supernet Training via Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Automating the design of efficient neural architectures can be accomplished effectively through weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS). This paradigm constructs a supernet whose sub-networks correspond to all candidate architectures, and the supernet is trained together with those sub-networks. Distilling the supernet's knowledge into the sub-networks is central to whether weight-sharing NAS performs well. We observe, however, that KL divergence—the divergence commonly employed during distillation—can cause the student sub-networks to over-estimate or under-estimate the teacher supernet's uncertainty, which degrades sub-network performance. To address this, our work turns to a broader alpha-divergence for training the supernet. Choosing the alpha-divergence in an adaptive manner lets us guard against both under-estimation and over-estimation of the teacher model's uncertainty at once. We deploy this alpha-divergence-based supernet training in the settings of slimmable neural networks as well as weight-sharing NAS, and observe substantial gains. In particular, the family of models we uncover surpasses prior-art approaches across a broad span of FLOPs budgets, such as BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. With just 444M FLOPs we reach a top-1 accuracy of 80.0% on ImageNet. Pretrained models and code can be found at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Extending Fake Media Detection Across Domains through Continual Representation and Distillation
abstract: Although artificial intelligence research has advanced enormously across recent decades, it continues to depend largely on static datasets within unchanging settings. As an expanding area of study, continual learning investigates how AI systems, mirroring biological ones, might acquire knowledge progressively from an ongoing flow of connected data. In parallel, fake media—including deepfakes and synthetic face images—have become highly relevant to today's multimedia technologies. A number of recently introduced techniques achieve high accuracy in identifying deepfakes; yet these approaches are considerably hindered by depending on fixed datasets tested under narrow conditions. In response, this work brings continual learning into the learning dynamics of neural networks, highlighting how it may substantially improve data efficiency. We introduce the proposed method, which draws on Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). The proposed method is built to carry out sequential domain adaptation across new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, all while curbing catastrophic forgetting within a teacher-student model configuration. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that our approach adapts efficiently across domains to spot low-quality deepfake videos and GAN-generated images drawn from multiple datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art baseline methods.

author: Maddox
title: Compressing BERT via Earth Mover's Distance and Many-to-Many Layer Mapping
abstract: Across a range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, pre-trained language models such as BERT have delivered notable gains. Their deployment on devices with limited resources is nonetheless hindered by demanding memory footprints and heavy computation. We introduce a new distillation approach for BERT grounded in many-to-many layer mapping, whereby every intermediate student layer is permitted to draw on any of the intermediate teacher layers. Through this scheme, the model adaptively absorbs knowledge from distinct teacher layers according to the NLP task at hand. We additionally employ Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to determine the least total cost required to move knowledge out of the teacher network and into the student network, which yields an effective way to align the many-to-many layer mapping. Beyond this, we put forward a cost attention mechanism that automatically learns the layer weights entering the EMD computation, with the aim of boosting performance further and shortening convergence time. On the GLUE benchmark, thorough experiments show that our approach reaches competitive results against strong baselines with respect to both accuracy and the degree of model compression.

author: Valencia
title: Shrinking Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
abstract: Deep learning models have driven remarkable advances across natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) over the past several years. Among them are Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) networks, as well as Transformer [120] based architectures such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98], and GShard [63]. Nevertheless, the sheer scale of these models poses a challenge, since deployment in practical settings requires compact models, rapid response, and modest computational power. This survey examines six categories of techniques—Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and Sub-quadratic Transformer based methods—aimed at compressing such models so they can be integrated into real industry NLP projects. In light of the pressing demand for compact and efficient models, together with the abundance of recent research on the topic, we aim to bring structure to the extensive contributions made by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in recent years and to relate them as a unified narrative.

author: Smith
title: Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks via Architecture Search
abstract: Because Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are increasingly being deployed on mobile devices for a wide range of purposes—among them image translation, enhancement, and editing—reducing their size has recently become a topic of interest. Yet, when set against the considerable work devoted to shrinking other deep models, studies on compressing GANs (typically their generators) are still nascent. The GAN compression methods available today can only cope with particular GAN architectures and losses. Drawing on the recent achievements of AutoML for deep compression, we bring AutoML to bear on GAN compression and build the proposed framework. Given constraints on the target computational resources, the method begins from a purpose-built efficient search space and carries out an end-to-end search for novel efficient generators. Knowledge distillation from the original GAN model steers this search, which is how the compression is achieved. The method operates without any human intervention, runs on its own (that is, it requires no trained discriminators), and applies broadly across different GAN models. Two representative GAN tasks, image translation and super resolution, serve as our testbeds. With no extra tricks, the method produces strikingly compact yet more competitive compressed models that substantially surpass current alternatives. We provide our codes and pretrained models at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Reconsidering Video-Pose embeddings for the understanding of Activities of Daily Living
abstract: The task of recognizing Activities of Daily Living (ADL) has frequently been approached by fusing RGB with 3D poses. Since distinct ADL can appear alike, capturing fine-grained details is often required to tell them apart. This line of work is largely governed by RGB-plus-3D-Pose techniques, owing to the fact that recent 3D ConvNets lack the flexibility needed to pick up the subtle visual cues that unfold during an action. However, when suitable sensors are unavailable, deriving 3D poses from the RGB stream carries a heavy computational burden, which restricts the applicability of such methods in low-latency real-world settings. This raises the question of how 3D Poses can be most effectively leveraged for ADL recognition. We address it by building upon a pose driven attention mechanism, the Video-Pose Network (VPN), and pursue two separate avenues. The first conveys Pose knowledge into RGB via a feature-level distillation, while the second reproduces pose driven attention using an attention-level distillation. We then unite both avenues within a single architecture, referred to here as the proposed method. Our results demonstrate that it is both effective and, in addition, delivers a substantial speed up together with strong robustness to noisy Poses. Whether or not 3D Poses are supplied, the proposed method surpasses the representative baselines across 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Transferring Knowledge Through Feature Imitation
abstract: To build efficient networks (the "student") with guidance from high-capacity networks (the "teacher"), knowledge distillation (KD) has become a widely adopted approach. Conventionally, the soft logits produced by the teacher serve as auxiliary supervision during student training. Here, we contend that having the student replicate the teacher's features at the penultimate layer offers greater benefits. Beyond enabling the student to absorb richer information directly from the teacher feature, this feature mimicking strategy also works when the teacher lacks a softmax layer. Our experiments demonstrate accuracy gains over conventional KD. To better support feature mimicking, we split a feature vector into its magnitude and its direction. Our position is that the student should have looser constraints on feature magnitude and instead concentrate on reproducing the feature direction. Toward this end, we introduce a loss term grounded in locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). This loss allows our method to reproduce feature directions with greater fidelity, loosen restrictions on feature magnitudes, and reach state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We supply theoretical analyses explaining why LSH aids feature direction mimicking, and additionally apply feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

author: Herrera
title: Reducing the Size of GANs through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Tasks like domain transfer, super resolution, and the creation of synthetic data have all been addressed with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Because leading GANs frequently rely on parameter counts in the tens of millions, they become costly to run in settings that demand real time responsiveness or on constrained low SWAP (size, weight, and power) platforms such as mobile devices. To our knowledge, cutting the parameter count of GANs has not previously been attempted. We accordingly introduce a scheme that applies knowledge distillation to shrink GANs, whereby a compact "student" GAN is trained to imitate a bulkier "teacher" GAN. On the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets, the distillation we employ achieves teacher GAN compression ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, without degrading the fidelity of the produced images. Our experiments reveal a qualitative ceiling on how far a GAN can be compressed. We further find that, under a fixed parameter budget, GANs obtained via compression surpass GANs produced by conventional training procedures. Part of the explanation, we suspect, lies in the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs, which lends itself to efficient training through alternating gradient descent. Consequently, first training an over-parameterized GAN and then applying our proposed compression yields a strong generative model that uses few parameters.

author: Davidson
title: Building Robustness into Re-Identification through Knowledge Distillation across Multiple Views
abstract: Conventional approaches to Re-Identification pursue robustness by exploiting tracking cues under a Video-To-Video paradigm. The downside is a substantial performance loss when only a single image serves as the query, such as in the Image-To-Video setting. To counter this pronounced deterioration, recent studies migrate temporal cues from a Video-based network into an Image-based counterpart. Here, we design a training procedure capable of conveying richer knowledge, which originates from several views portraying the target object. The method we propose treats this diversity of appearances as a supervisory signal inside a teacher-student setup: the student, exposed to a reduced number of views, is instructed by the teacher. Consequently, the student surpasses both its own teacher and the prevailing state-of-the-art for Image-To-Video by a considerable margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776). We conduct an extensive study spanning Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-ID, probing the characteristics of the proposed method from both qualitative and quantitative angles. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Differentially Private Publication of Trained Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are being adopted widely across delicate domains such as medicine and healthcare, which has prompted worries about how private a trained GNN really is. Notably, when adversaries have only black-box access to a trained model, they can still mount privacy attacks against GNNs, including membership inference attacks. For releasing GNN models under a centralized regime, we introduce a framework that preserves privacy. Given the availability of a public graph without labels, the proposed method offers a way to publish GNN models that are trained directly on public data while incorporating, in a privacy preserving fashion, knowledge derived from private data. To guarantee stringent privacy, the approach unites the knowledge-distillation framework with two mechanisms for adding noise: random subsampling and noisy labeling. We provide a theoretical treatment of the method within the Renyi differential privacy framework. In addition, against a range of baselines that we tailored to graph-structured data, our method demonstrates strong empirical results. We release our code at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

author: Graham
title: Regularization via Multi-Level Branching for Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning must contend with a key difficulty: the data held by different clients is imbalanced and heterogeneous, producing local networks that disagree with one another and global models whose convergence is unstable. We address these shortcomings with a new form of architectural regularization. Within every local model, the proposed method assembles several auxiliary branches by splicing together local and global subnetworks at a variety of levels; through online knowledge distillation, the representations along the local model's main pathway are then trained to agree with those of the auxiliary hybrid pathways. This approach strengthens the global model even under non-iid conditions, and it slots easily into a range of federated learning frameworks while adding no communication overhead. Our extensive experiments reveal substantial improvements in both accuracy and efficiency relative to prior approaches. We release the source code on our project page.

author: Chavez
title: Compressing Deep Neural Networks Through Knowledge Distillation Without Data
abstract: Techniques developed lately for model compression make it possible to shrink sizable neural networks down to a small portion of what they were originally, all while preserving nearly or entirely their accuracy. The catch is that every one of these methods depends on having the original training set available, a requirement that cannot always be satisfied: the network in question may have been trained on an enormous dataset, or on one that cannot be released owing to privacy or safety issues, as is frequently true in biometrics applications. Here we introduce an approach to knowledge distillation that requires no data, enabling deep neural networks trained over large-scale datasets to be reduced to a small portion of their size by relying solely on a bit of supplementary metadata shipped alongside a released pretrained model. We further investigate several varieties of metadata compatible with the proposed method and examine the tradeoffs that come with each choice.

author: Mckay
title: Toward Compute-Efficient Distillation for Large-scale Language Models via Mixup Augmentation
abstract: Strong empirical results have lately been reported by large-scale language models. These gains, however, come bundled with enlarged model sizes, heavier energy demands, and increased inference latency, all of which restrict deployment on platforms constrained in memory and computation. To shrink such heavy models, knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a useful framework. That said, systems built on large-scale neural networks are inclined to memorize their training instances, so their predictions can become unstable under even slight shifts in the data distribution. A further difficulty is that, when task-specific data is scarce, the student model rarely gets the chance to elicit informative signals from the teacher model. We tackle these problems with the proposed method, a data-agnostic distillation framework that draws on mixup—an uncomplicated yet effective form of data augmentation—to grant the trained model improved generalization ability. In practice, beyond the original training examples, the student model is also driven to reproduce the teacher's outputs on linearly interpolated pairs of examples. From a theoretical standpoint, we show that, given reasonable assumptions, the proposed method narrows the gap separating the generalization error from the empirical error. We validate the approach through experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where it reliably yields substantial improvements relative to standard KD training and surpasses several competitive baselines. Its benefits are further supported by ablation studies and by evaluations conducted in a limited-data regime.

author: Liu
title: Equipping CLIP for Multimodal Generation through Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Trained on enormous collections of image-text pairs, dual-stream architectures for vision-language pre-training (VLP) such as CLIP have recently demonstrated strong results across a range of multimodal alignment tasks. A limitation persists, however: because their text encoder is weak, these models cannot perform multimodal generative tasks. We address this by combining a dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM), using vision-language knowledge distillation to unlock multimodal generation capability. Relative to pre-training everything from scratch, this distillation approach demands far less data and computation. According to our experiments, the resulting model performs well in a zero-shot setting on multimodal generative tasks including image captioning and open-ended visual question answering. As an illustration, on the VQAv2 dataset it reaches 44.5% zero-shot accuracy, which exceeds the prior best zero-shot model while employing $7\times$ fewer parameters. In addition, the PLM retains its native abilities in textual language understanding and generation once distillation is complete, so our model can flexibly handle unimodal as well as multimodal tasks.

author: Mason
title: Training Student Networks through Feature Embedding
abstract: Although deep convolutional neural networks now serve a broad range of applications, the heavy demands they place on storage and computation stand in the way of deploying them on mobile devices. The goal of knowledge distillation is to tune a compact student network by transferring what a large, thoroughly trained teacher network has learned. Earlier teacher-student approaches typically depended on extra fully-connected layers to link the intermediate layers of the teacher and student networks, a strategy that introduces many auxiliary parameters. Here, by contrast, our aim is to carry information from teacher to student while avoiding the addition of any new variables requiring optimization. We reinterpret the teacher-student paradigm through the lens of feature embedding. A locality preserving loss guides the student network toward producing low-dimensional features that retain the intrinsic properties of the matching high-dimensional features generated by the teacher network. As a result, the compact network is able to preserve the teacher network's performance in a natural way. We include a theoretical analysis confirming that the proposed method has lower computation complexity. Across benchmark datasets and thoroughly trained networks, experiments indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods with respect to both computational and storage complexity.

author: White
title: Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks via Distillation for Lightweight Image Translation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have seen broad adoption across many image-to-image translation problems, yet their substantial demands on computation and memory make deployment on mobile devices difficult. While conventional approaches to network compression have targeted visual recognition, they have left generation tasks unaddressed. Drawing on the idea of knowledge distillation, we train a student generator with a reduced parameter count so that it absorbs both the low-level and high-level information carried by the bulky original teacher generator. We further introduce a student discriminator that quantifies how far apart real images lie from those produced by the student and teacher generators, thereby boosting the student generator's ability. This gives rise to an adversarial learning procedure that jointly optimizes the student generator alongside the student discriminator. Experiments carried out on benchmark datasets, evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively, show that the proposed method yields portable generative models exhibiting strong performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-Adaptive Compression of BERT via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Across a range of natural language processing tasks, sizeable pre-trained language models like BERT have proven effective. Their enormous parameter count, nonetheless, is an obstacle to deploying them in real-time settings where fast inference must occur under constrained resources. Prior work shrinks BERT down to compact models, yet these approaches are task-independent, producing one identical compressed BERT that serves every downstream task alike. Because task-oriented BERT compression is both needed and advantageous, we introduce a new compression technique that applies differentiable Neural Architecture Search to derive, in an automatic fashion, task-adaptive small models tailored to individual tasks. Search hints come from a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss we incorporate, while an efficiency-aware loss serves as a search constraint, together yielding a favorable balance between efficiency and effectiveness in task-adaptive BERT compression. Testing the proposed method on several NLP tasks, our findings show these task-adaptive compressed models achieve inference speeds 12.7x to 29.3x greater than BERT and shrink parameter size by 11.5x to 17.0x, all while preserving comparable performance.

author: Harrell
title: Nobody Excluded: Federated Learning That Embraces Diverse Device Capabilities
abstract: To build a shared global model from data spread across many sources while safeguarding privacy, federated learning (FL) has become a key approach. A common presumption behind current FL techniques is that every participating client is capable of training the global model. Yet in practice the hardware owned by clients varies widely, offering unequal computing power. Large models such as BERT, despite their remarkable achievements in AI, are hard to deploy in heterogeneous FL settings that include weak clients. Naive remedies—either dropping the weak clients or forcing a single small model onto everyone—raise their own difficulties, including under-representation of the excluded clients and reduced accuracy stemming from lost data or restricted model capacity. This paper introduces a client-inclusive FL method that addresses these issues. Its central concept is to match model size to client capability, giving larger models to more capable clients and smaller ones to weaker clients. We further devise an effective mechanism for sharing knowledge across the multiple local models of differing sizes. Through this design, every client can contribute to the FL training process, while the resulting model remains sufficiently large and powerful. In addition, we present a momentum knowledge distillation technique that improves how knowledge from the big models on powerful clients is transferred to the small models on weak clients. Comprehensive experiments across numerous real-world benchmark datasets confirm that the proposed method produces accurate models within the FL framework when clients possess heterogeneous devices.

author: Evans
title: Toward Space-Efficient Evaluation Metrics for Machine Translation
abstract: Trained metrics like COMET and BLEURT have gained traction among researchers following advances in machine translation and multilingual text generation; these approaches frame evaluation as regression and draw on representations produced by multilingual pre-trained models including mBERT or XLM-RoBERTa. Nevertheless, findings on comparable tasks indicate that such models perform best at large scale, an option that is expensive and unrealistic for evaluation purposes. Drawing on the WMT Metrics Shared Task data, we study how multilinguality and model capacity trade off against each other, using the state-of-the-art multilingual language model RemBERT. Through a sequence of experiments, we first establish that model size constitutes a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, and we then show that distillation offers a way to relieve this bottleneck by generating synthetic data and passing knowledge from a single teacher to several students, each trained on related languages. Compared with plain fine-tuning, the proposed method delivers gains as high as 10.5%, and it attains 92.6% of what RemBERT achieves while requiring only a third of the parameters.

author: Fowler
title: Transferring Self-supervised Visual Representations Through Distillation
abstract: The focus of this work is applying self-supervised learning to compact models. Our motivation stems from empirical observations: although contrastive self-supervised learning, now in common use, has advanced considerably for training large models, its effectiveness diminishes when applied to small ones. We introduce a novel learning paradigm to overcome this limitation, in which a bigger network, acting as the Teacher, conveys its representational knowledge to a more compact architecture, acting as the Student, under a self-supervised regime. Rather than having the student encoder learn straight from unlabeled data, we train it to reproduce the similarity score distribution that a teacher computes across a collection of instances. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method yields substantial gains for small networks on downstream tasks. Relative to self-supervised baselines, on the ImageNet-1k dataset the top-1 accuracy rises from 42.2% to 67.6% for EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% for MobileNet-v3-Large.

author: Lynch
title: Distilling Knowledge Across Modalities from Vision to Sensor for Recognizing Actions
abstract: Recent evidence indicates that multi-modal strategies can raise the accuracy of human activity recognition (HAR). Yet wearable hardware such as smartwatches offers limited computational resources, which prevents it from running these sophisticated techniques on its own. As a remedy, we present an end-to-end framework that distills knowledge from vision to sensor. Under the proposed framework, wearable devices are asked to supply only time-series signals—accelerometer readings—when the system is being tested. Consequently, the framework eases the computational burden placed on edge devices while yielding a learning model whose performance stays close to that of the costly multi-modal approach. To preserve the local temporal relationship and enable visual deep learning models, we begin by transforming the time-series data into two-dimensional images through an encoding scheme based on the Gramian Angular Field (GAF). For the teacher and student networks, respectively, we chose ResNet18 and a multi-scale TRN built on BN-Inception. We further introduce a new loss function—termed Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK)—designed to reduce the modality gap separating the sensor and vision domains. Comprehensive experiments across the UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets confirm that the proposed model is both effective and competitive, and that it is suitable for deployment on wearable sensors.

author: Hernandez
title: Efficient Novel View Synthesis by Distilling a Neural Radiance Field into a Neural Light Field
abstract: The surge of recent work on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) has demonstrated promising capacity for capturing intricate scenes through neural networks. A significant limitation, however, lies in NeRF's costly inference: producing one pixel demands hundreds of queries to the NeRF network. Prior work addresses this chiefly by cutting down the count of sampled points that are needed, yet the burden of iterative sampling remains. By contrast, for novel view synthesis a Neural Light Field (NeLF) offers a simpler representation than NeRF, since generating a pixel reduces to a single forward pass free of ray-marching. Here we introduce a deep residual MLP network with 88 layers to learn the light field effectively. We find that the crux of training such a deep NeLF network lies in having enough data, which we obtain by distilling data to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model. Comprehensive experiments across both real-world and synthetic scenes demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms competing algorithms. For synthetic scenes, we attain a 26-35x FLOPs reduction per camera ray together with a 28-31x runtime speedup, while at the same time producing markedly higher rendering quality than NeRF (an average PSNR gain of 1.4-2.8 dB), and doing so without demanding any customized parallelism.

author: Farmer
title: Knowledge Distillation for Building Efficient 3D Object Detectors
abstract: Advanced 3D detectors, notwithstanding considerable advances in 3D object detection, frequently incur substantial computational cost. Motivated by this, we investigate whether knowledge distillation (KD) can help construct efficient 3D object detectors, with an emphasis on widely used pillar- and voxel-based detectors. Because mature teacher-student pairs are not readily available, we begin by examining how student models that balance efficiency and accuracy can be derived, considering both the reduction of input resolution and the compression of models. Using six carefully designed teacher-student pairs, we then establish a benchmark that evaluates KD techniques originally proposed for the 2D setting when applied to 3D object detection.
