We additionally introduce an improved KD pipeline that combines two components: a refined logit KD scheme restricting distillation to a small set of critical locations identified via the teacher's classification response, and a teacher-guided initialization of the student that transfers the teacher's feature extraction capability to the student through weight inheritance. We finally carry out comprehensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Reaching $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH while consuming just $44\%$ of the teacher's flops, our top model exceeds the teacher it was distilled from. On an NVIDIA A100, our most efficient variant operates at 51 FPS, running $2.2\times$ quicker than PointPillar and with better accuracy. Code is released at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

author: Ryan
title: Distilling knowledge from multi-modal into mono-modal segmentation networks
abstract: Combining several imaging modalities for the segmentation of medical images has received considerable attention lately. Across a range of applications, merging the information carried by distinct modalities has been shown to yield better segmentation accuracy than relying on a single modality. Clinical practice, however, rarely permits the acquisition of multiple modalities: the shortage of physicians and scanners, together with the need to contain costs and scan time, typically restricts acquisition to just one modality. We introduce here a framework, the proposed method, that conveys knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (the teacher) toward a mono-modal counterpart (the student). This approach adapts the generalized distillation framework, having the student network learn from a subset (1 modality) of the n modalities that constitute the teacher's inputs. We demonstrate how well the framework performs on brain tumor segmentation using the BraTS 2018 dataset. Experiments with several architectures reveal that the student network learns effectively from the teacher and consistently surpasses the mono-modal baseline network with respect to segmentation accuracy.

author: Osborne
title: Transferring Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications in the Healthcare Field
abstract: The rapid, exponential expansion of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has created pressing demands and fresh possibilities in Computational Phenotyping research, where the aim is to uncover meaningful data-driven disease patterns and representations. Although Deep Learning models deliver strong performance and robust prediction on computational phenotyping tasks, they are hampered by limited model interpretability, a property that matters greatly to clinicians who must make decisions. Here we present a new knowledge-distillation technique, the proposed method, which acquires interpretable phenotype features that support robust prediction while reproducing the effectiveness of deep learning models. To distill interpretable features out of deep learning models like Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory, our framework relies on Gradient Boosting Trees. Through comprehensive experiments conducted on a real-world clinical time-series dataset, we demonstrate that performance matching or exceeding that of the deep learning models is achieved by our approach, along with interpretable phenotypes suited to clinical decision making.

author: Moreno
title: Acquiring Perception-Aware Agile Flight Through Obstacle-Dense Spaces
abstract: For flying quadrotors autonomously through obstacle-dense spaces in minimum time, neural control policies have lately surpassed the model-based planning-and-control approaches that came before. These policies, though, lack perception awareness—a property that matters greatly for vision-based navigation, given that a camera sees only a narrow field of view and that a quadrotor is underactuated. We introduce a learning-based system delivering agile, perception-aware flight amid clutter. By drawing on a privileged learning-by-cheating framework, the proposed method brings together imitation learning and reinforcement learning (RL). We begin by using RL to train, with access to full-state information, a perception-aware teacher policy capable of traversing cluttered environments in minimum time. Its knowledge is subsequently distilled through imitation learning into a vision-based student policy whose only sensing of the surroundings comes from a camera. Because our approach binds control and perception closely together, it yields a marked gain in success rate and in computation speed (a factor of 10). Closed-loop control performance is validated via hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

author: Smith
title: Adapting Then Distilling: Building Compact, Rapid, and Capable Pretrained Language Models Tailored to Domains
abstract: Across numerous natural language processing tasks, large pre-trained models have proven highly successful. Yet deploying them within particular domains introduces domain shift, and the resulting latency and capacity limits create difficulties for both fine-tuning and online serving. We describe here a broadly applicable methodology for producing pre-trained models that are small, fast and effective for a given domain. The idea rests on taking existing general pre-trained models off the shelf, adapting them, and then carrying out task-agnostic knowledge distillation on the target domain. In the adaptation phase, we introduce an expansion of the vocabulary specific to the domain, and the size of this added vocabulary is selected automatically by relying on corpus level occurrence probability. Following this, we investigate in a systematic manner a range of strategies for compressing the large pre-trained models toward specific domains. Our evaluation spans the computer science and biomedical domains. According to the experimental results, on domain-specific tasks the proposed method surpasses the BERT BASE model in performance while being 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. Both the code and the pre-trained models can be found at https://aka.ms/adalm.

author: Nguyen
title: Applying Knowledge Distillation to Compact Highway Networks
abstract: Over recent years, the leading results in speech recognition have been pushed forward considerably through deep learning. A drawback, though, is that neural network models tend to be far larger than the traditional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, which limits how readily they can run on embedded hardware. In earlier work, we studied a small highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, a variety of depth-gated feedforward neural network. That study demonstrated that acoustic models built on HDNN reach recognition accuracy on par with plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models while requiring far fewer model parameters. Here we extend those results by drawing on knowledge distillation, sometimes referred to as {\it teacher-student} training: the compact HDNN model is trained under the guidance of a bulky, highly accurate model. In addition, we explore sequence training as well as adaptation within the teacher-student framework. We ran experiments on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. Using this approach, the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model, which has fewer than 0.8 million parameters, improved substantially, closing the distance between it and the plain DNN carrying 30 million parameters.
